"""Exercise 2 - Binary classification a straight line cannot do.

Generates the three-blob dataset of the statement, fits the logistic-regression baseline, trains the
MLP of mlp.py with a sigmoid output and binary cross-entropy, and writes Figures 1, 2 and 3.

Every number quoted in the report is printed by this script. Run it from the repository root:

    python docs/exercises/mlp/code/exercise2_binary.py
"""

import math

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")  # no interactive display needed: we only save files
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

from common import COLORS, FIGURES, SEED, split
from mlp import MLP

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Setup: one seed, one generator, used for everything below
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

LAYER_SIZES = [2, 8, 1]   # 2 inputs, one hidden layer of 8 tanh units, 1 sigmoid output
LEARNING_RATE = 0.5
EPOCHS = 2000

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A - Generate the data (Figure 1), with the statement's parameters unchanged
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
centers = np.array([[0., 0.], [3., 3.], [-3., -3.]])
X, c = make_blobs(n_samples=[500, 250, 250], centers=centers,
                  cluster_std=1.2, random_state=42)
y = (c > 0).astype(int)      # class 0: 1 cluster | class 1: 2 clusters

# The blob index c is split alongside, only to read the results per cluster in items B and D.
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, c_train, c_test = split(X, y, c)

print("=== A - data ===")
print(f"samples: {len(X)} (class 0: {np.sum(y == 0)}, class 1: {np.sum(y == 1)}); "
      f"train {len(X_train)}, test {len(X_test)}")
for k in range(3):
    print(f"  blob {k} centred at {centers[k]}: {np.sum(c_train == k)} train / {np.sum(c_test == k)} test points")
print(f"class means (train): class 0 {X_train[y_train == 0].mean(axis=0).round(4)}, "
      f"class 1 {X_train[y_train == 1].mean(axis=0).round(4)}")

CLUSTER_NAMES = ["centre blob (0, 0)", "blob (3, 3)", "blob (-3, -3)"]


def scatter_classes(ax, X, y, **kwargs):
    """Scatter the two classes on `ax`, one colour each, with the axis labels every figure needs."""
    for k in (0, 1):
        ax.scatter(X[y == k, 0], X[y == k, 1], color=COLORS[k], label=f"Class {k} ({np.sum(y == k)} points)",
                   **kwargs)
    ax.set_xlabel("Feature 1 ($x_1$)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Feature 2 ($x_2$)")
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25, linestyle=":")


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 7))
scatter_classes(ax, X, y, s=12, alpha=0.6)
ax.set_title("Figure 1 - Exercise 2 data: class 1 is two blobs on opposite sides of class 0")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", framealpha=0.95)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIGURES / "fig1_data.png", dpi=150)
plt.close(fig)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# B - Baseline: one straight line (logistic regression, allowed here as the baseline only)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
baseline = LogisticRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
w, b = baseline.coef_[0], baseline.intercept_[0]
baseline_test = baseline.score(X_test, y_test)
p_test = baseline.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
pred_baseline = baseline.predict(X_test)


def phi(t):
    """Standard normal CDF."""
    return 0.5 * (1.0 + math.erf(t / math.sqrt(2.0)))


# Accuracy the fitted line would have on the generating distribution itself (an infinite test set): each
# blob is an isotropic Gaussian, so the share of it on the class-1 side of w.x + b = 0 is a normal CDF.
share_positive = [phi((w @ mu + b) / (1.2 * np.linalg.norm(w))) for mu in centers]
expected_accuracy = 0.5 * (1 - share_positive[0]) + 0.25 * share_positive[1] + 0.25 * share_positive[2]

print("\n=== B - linear baseline ===")
print(f"w = {w.round(4)}, b = {b:.4f}; |w| = {np.linalg.norm(w):.4f}; "
      f"angle of w {np.degrees(np.arctan2(w[1], w[0])):.2f} deg; line offset -b/|w| = {-b / np.linalg.norm(w):.4f}")
print(f"train accuracy {baseline.score(X_train, y_train):.2%}, TEST ACCURACY {baseline_test:.2%} "
      f"({int(round(baseline_test * len(y_test)))} of {len(y_test)})")
print(f"P(class 1) on the test points ranges over [{p_test.min():.4f}, {p_test.max():.4f}]")
for k in range(3):
    s = c_test == k
    print(f"  {CLUSTER_NAMES[k]:<16}: {s.sum():3d} test points, {pred_baseline[s].mean():.0%} predicted class 1, "
          f"{np.sum(pred_baseline[s] == y_test[s])} correct")
print(f"expected accuracy of this line on the generating distribution: {expected_accuracy:.2%}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# C - The MLP (mlp.py), trained with full-batch gradient descent (Figures 2 and 3)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
model = MLP(LAYER_SIZES, output="sigmoid", rng=rng)
history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=EPOCHS, learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE)
mlp_test = model.accuracy(X_test, y_test)
pred_mlp = model.predict(X_test)

print("\n=== C - MLP ===")
print(f"architecture {LAYER_SIZES} (tanh hidden, sigmoid output, binary cross-entropy), "
      f"{model.n_parameters} parameters; learning rate {LEARNING_RATE}; {EPOCHS} epochs of full-batch GD")
print(f"training loss: {history[0]:.4f} at epoch 0 -> {history[100]:.4f} at epoch 100 -> "
      f"{history[500]:.4f} at epoch 500 -> {history[-1]:.4f} at epoch {EPOCHS}")
print(f"train accuracy {model.accuracy(X_train, y_train):.2%}, TEST ACCURACY {mlp_test:.2%} "
      f"({int(round(mlp_test * len(y_test)))} of {len(y_test)})")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
ax.plot(np.arange(EPOCHS + 1), history, color="black", linewidth=1.6, label=f"MLP {LAYER_SIZES}, $\\eta$ = {LEARNING_RATE}")
ax.set_title("Figure 2 - Exercise 2: training loss (binary cross-entropy) per epoch")
ax.set_xlabel("Epoch")
ax.set_ylabel("Training loss (binary cross-entropy)")
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
ax.grid(alpha=0.3, linestyle=":")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIGURES / "fig2_loss.png", dpi=150)
plt.close(fig)

# Decision regions: evaluate the network on a grid and shade where P(class 1) >= 0.5.
lim = 7.5
g1, g2 = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-lim, lim, 601), np.linspace(-lim, lim, 601))
P_grid = model.predict_proba(np.c_[g1.ravel(), g2.ravel()])[:, 0].reshape(g1.shape)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 7.5))
ax.contourf(g1, g2, P_grid, levels=[0, 0.5, 1], colors=[COLORS[0], COLORS[1]], alpha=0.18)
ax.contour(g1, g2, P_grid, levels=[0.5], colors="black", linewidths=1.6)
scatter_classes(ax, X_test, y_test, s=22, alpha=0.85, edgecolors="white", linewidths=0.4)
wrong = pred_mlp != y_test
ax.scatter(X_test[wrong, 0], X_test[wrong, 1], s=70, facecolors="none", edgecolors="black", linewidths=1.0)
xs = np.linspace(-lim, lim, 2)  # the baseline's line, solved for x1 since it is nearly vertical
ax.plot(-(w[1] * xs + b) / w[0], xs, color="dimgray", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.4)
ax.set_xlim(-lim, lim)
ax.set_ylim(-lim, lim)
handles, labels = ax.get_legend_handles_labels()
handles += [Patch(color=COLORS[0], alpha=0.3), Patch(color=COLORS[1], alpha=0.3),
            plt.Line2D([], [], color="black", linewidth=1.6),
            plt.Line2D([], [], marker="o", linestyle="", markerfacecolor="none", markeredgecolor="black"),
            plt.Line2D([], [], color="dimgray", linestyle="--")]
labels += ["MLP region: class 0", "MLP region: class 1", "MLP boundary P(class 1) = 0.5",
           f"Misclassified by the MLP ({wrong.sum()})", f"Linear baseline boundary ({baseline_test:.1%})"]
ax.legend(handles, labels, loc="upper left", framealpha=0.95, fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_title(f"Figure 3 - MLP decision regions over the {len(X_test)} test points "
             f"(test accuracy {mlp_test:.1%})", fontsize=10.5)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIGURES / "fig3_boundary.png", dpi=150)
plt.close(fig)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# D - Analysis: the shape of the class-1 region
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Walk along the diagonal through the three centres, t (1, 1)/sqrt(2), and along the perpendicular
# anti-diagonal t (1, -1)/sqrt(2), and record where the network's prediction changes.
t = np.linspace(-lim * np.sqrt(2), lim * np.sqrt(2), 20001)
on_diagonal = model.predict(np.c_[t, t] / np.sqrt(2))
crossings = t[np.flatnonzero(np.diff(on_diagonal))]
on_antidiagonal = model.predict(np.c_[t, -t] / np.sqrt(2))

print("\n=== D - analysis ===")
print(f"along the diagonal (distance t from the origin) the prediction changes at t = {crossings.round(3)}")
print(f"  i.e. class 1 for t < {crossings[0]:.3f} and t > {crossings[-1]:.3f}: a class-0 band of width "
      f"{crossings[-1] - crossings[0]:.3f} around the anti-diagonal")
print(f"along the anti-diagonal (|t| <= {t.max():.1f}): {on_antidiagonal.mean():.0%} predicted class 1")
print(f"midpoint of the two class-1 centres, (0, 0): predicted class {model.predict(np.zeros((1, 2)))[0]}")

# Reference, not fitted: projected on the diagonal, class 0 is N(0, 1.2^2) with weight 1/2 and each class-1
# blob is N(+-3 sqrt2, 1.2^2) with weight 1/4. The best possible boundary sits where the weighted densities
# cross (the far blob's contribution there is negligible), and its accuracy is the best any model can expect.
d = 3 * np.sqrt(2)
t_bayes = d / 2 + 1.2 ** 2 * np.log(2) / d
bayes_accuracy = 0.5 * (2 * phi(t_bayes / 1.2) - 1) + 0.5 * (1 - phi((t_bayes - d) / 1.2))
print(f"Bayes-optimal boundary: t = +-{t_bayes:.3f} along the diagonal; expected accuracy {bayes_accuracy:.2%}")
for k in range(3):
    s = c_test == k
    print(f"  {CLUSTER_NAMES[k]:<16}: MLP correct on {np.sum(pred_mlp[s] == y_test[s])} of {s.sum()} "
          f"({np.mean(pred_mlp[s] == y_test[s]):.1%})")

docs.title: D — Analysis
docs.text:
The region the MLP assigns to class 1 (Figure 3) is two disconnected pieces:

  • the pieces lie in the upper right and the lower left;
  • a band of class 0 runs along the anti-diagonal between them;
  • walking along the diagonal through the three centres, the prediction switches at \(t = -2.276\) and \(t = +2.331\) from the origin, so the band is 4.61 wide;
  • along the anti-diagonal, the network predicts class 0 everywhere (0% class 1).

For reference, the best possible boundary for these Gaussians is the pair of lines at \(t = \pm 2.357\), with an expected accuracy of 94.62%. The network found it almost exactly. Its 17 test errors are points that fell on the wrong side of an overlap, such as class-1 points inside the band. They are not a flaw in the shape of the region.

Why no single straight line can produce that region. A line splits the plane into two half-planes, so a linear classifier's class-1 region is a half-plane \(\{\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b > 0\}\), and a half-plane is convex. Convexity is what rules it out:

  • any convex set that contains the centre of the blob at \((3, 3)\) and the centre of the blob at \((-3, -3)\) must contain the whole segment between them;
  • that segment passes through \((0, 0)\), the centre of class 0;
  • the class-1 region a correct classifier needs contains both blob centres but not \((0, 0)\) (the MLP predicts class 0 there), so it is not convex, and no single line can draw it.

The best any line can do is to give up one outer blob completely, for about 75% at most.

Why the baseline does even worse, below 50%. It has two causes.

  1. Logistic regression does not even look for that 75% line. It minimises cross-entropy, not errors, and this data is symmetric: both classes have their mean at the origin. The training means are \((0.02, 0.05)\) for class 0 and \((0.21, 0.20)\) for class 1. A linear score \(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b\) can only reward a direction in which one class sits higher on average, and here there is none. Tilting the line towards one outer blob costs as much cross-entropy on the opposite blob as it gains. The fit therefore stays flat: \(\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert = 0.0297\), and every predicted probability lies between 0.4566 and 0.5438.
  2. The small slope that is left comes from a sample imbalance, and that imbalance is reversed in the test set.
    • The blob at \((3, 3)\) received 208 training points against 192 for \((-3, -3)\), which pulls the class-1 mean slightly towards \((3, 3)\).
    • The fitted line is nearly vertical, at \(x_1 \approx 0.10\) (the dashed line in Figure 3), and it predicts class 1 to its right.
    • On the test set, the line classifies all 42 points of blob \((3, 3)\) correctly, none of the 58 points of blob \((-3, -3)\), and 53 of the 100 centre points: \((42 + 0 + 53)/200 = 47.5\%\).
    • Each blob has exactly 250 points, so the blob that is over-represented in training is necessarily under-represented in the test set: \(250 - 208 = 42 < 58\). The line favours the blob that the test set has fewer of.
    • On the generating distribution itself, the same line would score 51.68%. The drop to 47.5% is that train/test complement.

What the hidden layer adds. Each of the 8 hidden units computes a soft line, \(\tanh(\mathbf{w}_j\cdot\mathbf{x} + b_j)\). The output layer combines them, and a combination of lines can describe a non-convex region: here, everything outside a band. That one capability is the difference between 47.5% and 91.5%.

docs.title: B — Adapt the network
docs.text:
The network is the same MLP class, imported from the same mlp.py. Only the constructor arguments change:

model = MLP([2, 8, 1], output="sigmoid", rng=rng)    # Exercise 2: 1 output, sigmoid + binary cross-entropy
model = MLP([4, 16, 3], output="softmax", rng=rng)   # Exercise 3: 3 outputs, softmax + categorical cross-entropy

With three output units, softmax turns the three scores into probabilities and categorical cross-entropy replaces binary cross-entropy:

\[ p_k = \frac{e^{u_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^3 e^{u_j}}, \qquad L = -\sum_{k=1}^3 y_k \log p_k \quad (\mathbf{y} \text{ one-hot}). \]

Deriving \(\partial L/\partial \mathbf{u}\). The derivative of the softmax couples every output with every score:

\[ \frac{\partial p_k}{\partial u_j} = \frac{e^{u_k}\,[k = j]\,\sum_m e^{u_m} - e^{u_k}e^{u_j}}{\big(\sum_m e^{u_m}\big)^2} = p_k\big([k = j] - p_j\big). \]

The chain rule through the loss then gives

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial u_j} = -\sum_k \frac{y_k}{p_k}\,\frac{\partial p_k}{\partial u_j} = -\sum_k y_k\big([k = j] - p_j\big) = -y_j + p_j \sum_k y_k = \boxed{\,p_j - y_j\,}, \]

because a one-hot \(\mathbf{y}\) sums to 1.

Why it is so simple. The logarithm of the loss undoes the exponential of the softmax. If \(c\) is the true class, \(\log p_c = u_c - \log\sum_j e^{u_j}\), so

\[ L = -u_c + \log\sum_j e^{u_j}, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial u_j} = -[j = c] + \frac{e^{u_j}}{\sum_m e^{u_m}} = p_j - y_j . \]

The loss is linear in the true class's score, plus a log-sum-exp whose gradient is the softmax itself. Sigmoid with binary cross-entropy is the two-class case of the same pairing, and it gave the same \(p - y\) in item 2C.

Verbatim reuse (extra point). Because both pairs give \(\boldsymbol\delta^{(L)} = (\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{Y})/N\), MLP.forward, MLP.backward and MLP.update serve Exercise 3 untouched. Three things are arguments, not code: the output size (3), the output activation and its loss (output="softmax"), and the hyperparameters. In the git history, mlp.py is committed once, before Exercise 2, and is never modified by the Exercise 3 or Exercise 4 commits. gradient_check.py confirms the gradients of the softmax network against finite differences.

exercise3_multiclass.py
"""Exercise 3 - Multi-class, same network.

Trains the MLP of mlp.py - the very same class as Exercise 2, now built with three output units and
output="softmax" - on the 4-feature, 3-class dataset of the statement. Fits the logistic-regression
baseline, writes Figures 4, 5 and 5b, and recovers the six generating clusters to explain the
confusion matrix (item D).

Every number quoted in the report is printed by this script. Run it from the repository root:

    python docs/exercises/mlp/code/exercise3_multiclass.py
"""

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")  # no interactive display needed: we only save files
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

from common import COLORS, EPOCHS, FIGURES, LEARNING_RATE, MULTICLASS_HIDDEN, SEED, multiclass_data, split
from mlp import MLP

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Setup: one seed, one generator, used for everything below
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

LAYER_SIZES = [4, *MULTICLASS_HIDDEN, 3]   # 4 inputs, one hidden layer of 16 tanh units, 3 softmax outputs

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A - Generate the data, with the statement's parameters unchanged
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
X, y = multiclass_data()

# make_classification does not say which of the 6 clusters each sample came from, and item D needs it.
# With shuffle=False the same generator returns the same samples, before the final shuffle, in cluster
# order: 250 samples per cluster, cluster k having label k % 3. The shuffle also permutes the columns,
# so each shuffled row is matched to its unshuffled copy by its sorted values.
X_ordered, y_ordered = multiclass_data(shuffle=False)
cluster_of = {tuple(np.sort(row).round(10)): i // 250 for i, row in enumerate(X_ordered)}
assert len(cluster_of) == len(X), "two samples share the same values"
cluster = np.array([cluster_of[tuple(np.sort(row).round(10))] for row in X])
assert np.all(np.bincount(cluster) == 250)
label_of = {tuple(np.sort(row).round(10)): label for row, label in zip(X_ordered, y_ordered)}
assert all(label_of[tuple(np.sort(row).round(10))] == label for row, label in zip(X, y))
flipped = y != cluster % 3  # make_classification flips ~1% of the labels at random (flip_y=0.01)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, c_train, c_test = split(X, y, cluster)

print("=== A - data ===")
print(f"samples: {len(X)}, features: {X.shape[1]}, per class: {np.bincount(y)}; "
      f"train {len(X_train)} {np.bincount(y_train)}, test {len(X_test)} {np.bincount(y_test)}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# B - Adapt the network: the same MLP class, three output units and output="softmax"
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
model = MLP(LAYER_SIZES, output="softmax", rng=rng)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# C - Train and evaluate (Figures 4 and 5)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=EPOCHS, learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE)
mlp_test = model.accuracy(X_test, y_test)
pred = model.predict(X_test)
C = confusion_matrix(y_test, pred)

print("\n=== C - MLP ===")
print(f"architecture {LAYER_SIZES} (tanh hidden, softmax output, categorical cross-entropy), "
      f"{model.n_parameters} parameters; learning rate {LEARNING_RATE}; {EPOCHS} epochs of full-batch GD")
print(f"training loss: {history[0]:.4f} at epoch 0 -> {history[100]:.4f} at epoch 100 -> "
      f"{history[500]:.4f} at epoch 500 -> {history[-1]:.4f} at epoch {EPOCHS}")
print(f"train accuracy {model.accuracy(X_train, y_train):.2%}, TEST ACCURACY {mlp_test:.2%} "
      f"({np.trace(C)} of {C.sum()})")
print("confusion matrix (rows = true class, columns = predicted class):")
print(C)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
ax.plot(np.arange(EPOCHS + 1), history, color="black", linewidth=1.6,
        label=f"MLP {LAYER_SIZES}, $\\eta$ = {LEARNING_RATE}")
ax.set_title("Figure 4 - Exercise 3: training loss (categorical cross-entropy) per epoch")
ax.set_xlabel("Epoch")
ax.set_ylabel("Training loss (categorical cross-entropy)")
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
ax.grid(alpha=0.3, linestyle=":")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIGURES / "fig4_loss.png", dpi=150)
plt.close(fig)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.4))
image = ax.imshow(C, cmap="Blues")
for i in range(3):
    for j in range(3):
        ax.text(j, i, C[i, j], ha="center", va="center", fontsize=14,
                color="white" if C[i, j] > C.max() / 2 else "black")
class_names = [f"Class {k}" for k in range(3)]
ax.set_xticks(range(3), class_names)
ax.set_yticks(range(3), class_names)
ax.set_xlabel("Predicted class")
ax.set_ylabel("True class")
fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, label="Number of test samples")
ax.set_title(f"Figure 5 - Exercise 3: confusion matrix on the {C.sum()} test samples\n"
             f"(MLP {LAYER_SIZES}, test accuracy {mlp_test:.1%})", fontsize=10.5)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIGURES / "fig5_confusion.png", dpi=150)
plt.close(fig)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# D - Analysis: the most confused pair, the cluster structure behind it, and the linear baseline
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
pairs = {(a, b): int(C[a, b] + C[b, a]) for a, b in [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2)]}
worst = max(pairs, key=pairs.get)

print("\n=== D - analysis ===")
print("test samples confused, per class pair (both directions):",
      ", ".join(f"{a}<->{b}: {n}" for (a, b), n in pairs.items()))
print(f"most confused pair: classes {worst[0]} and {worst[1]} ({pairs[worst]} test samples)")
print(f"recall per class: {(np.diag(C) / C.sum(axis=1)).round(3)}")

# The clusters: centroid (sample mean), the sign pattern of its hypercube vertex, and its class.
centroids = np.array([X[cluster == k].mean(axis=0) for k in range(6)])
vertices = np.sign(centroids).astype(int)
print(f"\nlabels flipped by the generator: {flipped.sum()} of {len(y)} ({np.sum(y_test != c_test % 3)} in the test set)")
print("clusters (k: class, vertex, sample centroid, spread = singular values of the centred cluster / sqrt(n)):")
for k in range(6):
    spread = np.linalg.svd(X[cluster == k] - centroids[k], compute_uv=False) / np.sqrt(250)
    print(f"  cluster {k}: class {k % 3}, vertex {vertices[k]}, centroid {centroids[k].round(2)}, "
          f"spread {spread.round(2)}")

print("pairs of clusters of different classes on adjacent vertices (they differ in one coordinate):")
for i in range(6):
    for j in range(i + 1, 6):
        if i % 3 != j % 3 and np.sum(vertices[i] != vertices[j]) == 1:
            d = centroids[j] - centroids[i]
            u = d / np.linalg.norm(d)
            print(f"  cluster {i} (class {i % 3}) - cluster {j} (class {j % 3}): centroids {np.linalg.norm(d):.3f} apart, "
                  f"differ in feature x{np.flatnonzero(vertices[i] != vertices[j])[0] + 1}; std along the joining line "
                  f"{np.std(X[cluster == i] @ u):.3f} and {np.std(X[cluster == j] @ u):.3f}")

print("test samples per cluster, MLP predictions (columns = predicted class 0, 1, 2):")
for k in range(6):
    s = c_test == k
    print(f"  cluster {k} (class {k % 3}): {s.sum():3d} samples, predicted {np.bincount(pred[s], minlength=3)}, "
          f"{np.mean(pred[s] == y_test[s]):.1%} correct")
confused = ((y_test == worst[0]) & (pred == worst[1])) | ((y_test == worst[1]) & (pred == worst[0]))
print(f"origin of the {confused.sum()} test samples confused between classes {worst[0]} and {worst[1]}: "
      f"clusters {np.bincount(c_test[confused], minlength=6)}")


def gaussian_logpdf(X, mean, cov):
    """log N(x; mean, cov) up to the shared constant, for every row of X."""
    d = X - mean
    return -0.5 * np.sum(d * np.linalg.solve(cov, d.T).T, axis=1) - 0.5 * np.linalg.slogdet(cov)[1]


# Reference ceiling: an "oracle" that knows the cluster of every TRAINING sample - which the network is
# never told - fits one Gaussian per cluster on the training set and predicts the class whose two
# clusters make a test sample most likely. The confusions it still makes come from the data itself.
log_lik = np.stack([gaussian_logpdf(X_test, X_train[c_train == k].mean(axis=0), np.cov(X_train[c_train == k].T))
                    for k in range(6)], axis=1)
oracle_pred = np.stack([np.logaddexp(log_lik[:, k], log_lik[:, k + 3]) for k in range(3)], axis=1).argmax(axis=1)
C_oracle = confusion_matrix(y_test, oracle_pred)
print(f"\noracle (one Gaussian per cluster, cluster ids known): test accuracy {np.mean(oracle_pred == y_test):.2%}; "
      "confused per pair: " + ", ".join(f"{a}<->{b}: {C_oracle[a, b] + C_oracle[b, a]}" for a, b in pairs))
print(C_oracle)

# Linear baseline: multinomial logistic regression, one linear score per class.
baseline = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X_train, y_train)
pred_baseline = baseline.predict(X_test)
print(f"\nlogistic-regression baseline: train {baseline.score(X_train, y_train):.2%}, "
      f"TEST ACCURACY {baseline.score(X_test, y_test):.2%}; MLP gain {mlp_test - baseline.score(X_test, y_test):+.2%}")
for k in range(6):
    s = c_test == k
    print(f"  cluster {k} (class {k % 3}): baseline {np.mean(pred_baseline[s] == y_test[s]):5.1%} correct, "
          f"MLP {np.mean(pred[s] == y_test[s]):5.1%}")

# A linear model gives each class one convex region, so a class whose two clusters are joined by a
# segment that passes close to another class's cluster cannot be covered without covering that one too.
print("midpoint between the two clusters of a class: distance to its own centroids vs to the nearest other-class centroid")
for k in range(3):
    midpoint = (centroids[k] + centroids[k + 3]) / 2
    others = [j for j in range(6) if j % 3 != k]
    nearest = min(others, key=lambda j: np.linalg.norm(centroids[j] - midpoint))
    print(f"  class {k} (clusters {k} and {k + 3}): own {np.linalg.norm(centroids[k] - midpoint):.3f}, "
          f"nearest other cluster {nearest} (class {nearest % 3}) at {np.linalg.norm(centroids[nearest] - midpoint):.3f}")

# Figure 5b: the chain of clusters behind the confusion. Cluster 1 (class 1) differs from cluster 0
# (class 0) in one feature and from cluster 2 (class 2) in another; plotting those two features shows
# the three clusters side by side, with the test samples the MLP gets wrong circled.
f_a = np.flatnonzero(vertices[0] != vertices[1])[0]
f_b = np.flatnonzero(vertices[1] != vertices[2])[0]
assert np.sum(vertices[0] != vertices[1]) == 1 and np.sum(vertices[1] != vertices[2]) == 1
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 8))
for k in (0, 1, 2):
    s = cluster == k
    ax.scatter(X[s, f_a], X[s, f_b], s=10, alpha=0.35, color=COLORS[k % 3],
               label=f"Cluster {k} = class {k % 3}, vertex {vertices[k]}")
    ax.scatter(*centroids[k, [f_a, f_b]], s=180, marker="X", color=COLORS[k % 3], edgecolors="black")
in_chain = np.isin(c_test, [0, 1, 2]) & (pred != y_test)
ax.scatter(X_test[in_chain, f_a], X_test[in_chain, f_b], s=60, facecolors="none", edgecolors="black",
           linewidths=1.0, label=f"Test samples of these clusters misclassified by the MLP ({in_chain.sum()})")
ax.scatter([], [], s=120, marker="X", color="lightgray", edgecolors="black", label="Cluster centroid")
ax.set_xlabel(f"Feature $x_{f_a + 1}$ (the one coordinate where clusters 0 and 1 differ)")
ax.set_ylabel(f"Feature $x_{f_b + 1}$ (the one coordinate where clusters 1 and 2 differ)")
ax.set_title("Figure 5b - Clusters 0, 1 and 2: one hypercube edge apart, overlapping", fontsize=11)
ax.grid(alpha=0.25, linestyle=":")
ax.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.1), fontsize=8.5, framealpha=0.95)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIGURES / "fig5b_clusters.png", dpi=150)
plt.close(fig)

docs.title: D — Analysis
docs.text:
The most confused pair is classes 0 and 1. The network mixes them up on 21 test samples: 9 samples of class 0 are predicted as 1 and 12 samples of class 1 as 0. The other pairs are less confused: 16 for classes 1 and 2, and 9 for classes 0 and 2. Class 1 has the lowest recall, 77%, against 88% and 89% for the other two classes.

The cluster structure. make_classification builds the data in four steps:

  1. It places the 6 clusters, 2 per class, on 6 of the 16 vertices of a 4-dimensional hypercube with side \(2 \times \texttt{class\_sep} = 2\), so every coordinate of a centre is \(\pm1\).
  2. It draws each cluster as a standard normal sample multiplied by its own random \(4\times4\) matrix, which gives every cluster a different, elongated shape.
  3. It flips 1% of the labels.
  4. It shuffles the rows and the columns.

After recovering each sample's cluster (decision 5 above), the recovered centroids sit at \(\pm1\) as expected:

Cluster Class Vertex Spread (std along its principal axes) Test samples correct 0 0 \((-,-,-,-)\) 1.90, 1.47, 0.68, 0.46 86.3% 1 1 \((-,+,-,-)\) 1.74, 1.67, 1.05, 0.67 61.2% 2 2 \((-,+,-,+)\) 1.90, 1.28, 0.80, 0.32 80.4% 3 0 \((+,-,+,+)\) 1.70, 1.58, 0.83, 0.15 89.8% 4 1 \((-,+,+,+)\) 1.35, 1.10, 0.48, 0.07 95.9% 5 2 \((+,+,+,-)\) 1.97, 1.26, 0.59, 0.43 92.9%

Two clusters on adjacent vertices differ in a single coordinate, so their centres are only 2 apart. Along the line joining them, each cluster spreads with a standard deviation of 0.9 to 1.4, so the two overlap heavily. Exactly three adjacent pairs belong to different classes:

Adjacent pair Classes Distance Std along the joining line clusters 0 – 1 0 / 1 2.032 (differ in \(x_2\)) 0.875 / 1.192 clusters 1 – 2 1 / 2 2.082 (differ in \(x_4\)) 1.367 / 1.121 clusters 2 – 4 2 / 1 1.917 (differ in \(x_3\)) 0.948 / 1.081

This structure explains the confusion matrix:

  • No class-0 cluster touches a class-2 cluster. That is why 0↔2 is the least confused pair, with 9 samples.
  • Cluster 1 is a hinge. It is the class-1 cluster adjacent to both a class-0 cluster (cluster 0) and a class-2 cluster (cluster 2), and it is the most spread-out cluster of all. Figure 5b shows it squeezed between the two. Only 61.2% of its test samples are classified correctly: 11 go to class 0 and 8 to class 2. Its leak towards cluster 0 is most of what keeps the recall of class 1 at 77%.
  • The 0↔1 confusion is the overlap between clusters 0 and 1. Of the 21 confused test samples, 18 come from those two clusters: 11 from cluster 1 and 7 from cluster 0. The remaining 3 come from clusters 2 and 3.
  • Why 0↔1 and not 1↔2. Classes 1 and 2 have two adjacencies, but the second one (clusters 2 – 4) barely overlaps. Cluster 4 is almost flat, with its smallest spread at 0.07, and 95.9% of its samples are classified correctly.

Figure 5b — clusters 0, 1 and 2 in the two coordinates where they differ: \(x_2\) separates clusters 0 and 1, and \(x_4\) separates clusters 1 and 2. Crosses mark the centroids. The circled points are the 35 test samples of these clusters that the MLP misclassifies. They fall where the clouds overlap.

How much of this the network could avoid. As a reference, an "oracle" knows the cluster of every training sample, which the network is never told. It fits one Gaussian per cluster and predicts the class whose two clusters make each test sample most likely. The oracle scores 89.33%, and it still confuses 12 test samples between classes 0 and 1 and 13 between classes 1 and 2:

  • that part of the overlap is in the data, not in the network;
  • the 2 test samples whose labels were flipped by the generator cannot be predicted by anyone;
  • the network's errors beyond the oracle's fall mostly on 0↔1: 21 against 12;
  • the ranking is stable across initializations: over the 10 seeds of Exercise 4, 0↔1 is the most confused pair in 8 of 10 runs of this architecture and in 9 of 10 runs of the deeper one.

The logistic-regression baseline and what the hidden layer added.

Model Test accuracy Logistic regression (multinomial) 66.33% (train 63.67%) MLP [4, 16, 3] 84.67% (+18.33 points)

A linear model gives each class one linear score and predicts the largest. The region it assigns to a class is therefore an intersection of half-spaces, which is convex. Each class here is two clusters at different vertices, and the segment between them runs close to clusters of other classes:

Class Its clusters Distance from the midpoint to its own centroids To the nearest other-class centroid 0 0 and 3 1.711 2.631 (cluster 1) 1 1 and 4 1.327 1.499 (cluster 2) 2 2 and 5 1.772 1.608 (cluster 1): closer than its own

A convex region that covers both clusters of class 2 must also cover much of cluster 1, and the reverse holds too. The baseline therefore has to give up whole clusters. It classifies correctly only 41.3% of cluster 2's test samples, 51.0% of cluster 1's and 65.3% of cluster 4's. Class 0, whose segment stays far from the other clusters, keeps about 80% on both of its clusters.

The hidden layer removes the convexity constraint. The tanh units carve out a separate region around each cluster, and the output layer then assigns both regions to the same class. The gains come exactly where the baseline was trapped:

  • cluster 2: 41.3% → 80.4%;
  • cluster 4: 65.3% → 95.9%;
  • cluster 5: 76.8% → 92.9%.

"""Exercise 4 - Does a second hidden layer help?

Same data, split, learning rate, number of epochs and initialization rule as Exercise 3; the only change
is one more hidden layer of the same width. Trains the deeper network with the seed used everywhere else
(item A), then trains both networks - and a one-layer control with the same parameter count as the
deeper one - from 10 seeds (item B), and writes Figure 6.

Every number quoted in the report is printed by this script. Run it from the repository root:

    python docs/exercises/mlp/code/exercise4_depth.py
"""

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")  # no interactive display needed: we only save files
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

from common import EPOCHS, FIGURES, LEARNING_RATE, MULTICLASS_HIDDEN, SEED, multiclass_data, split
from mlp import MLP

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Setup: one seed, one generator, used for everything below
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

SHALLOW = [4, *MULTICLASS_HIDDEN, 3]                      # Exercise 3: [4, 16, 3]
DEEP = [4, *MULTICLASS_HIDDEN, *MULTICLASS_HIDDEN, 3]     # Exercise 4: [4, 16, 16, 3], one more layer, same width
WIDE = [4, 50, 3]                                         # control, not asked: one layer, as many parameters as DEEP

# Item B asks for at least 3 seeds. Seed 42 - the one used for every other run in the report - comes
# first, so its runs are exactly the Exercise 3 network and the item-A network. The seed only changes
# the initial weights: the data and the split are the statement's, fixed by random_state=42.
SEEDS = list(range(42, 52))

X, y = multiclass_data()
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = split(X, y)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A - Train the deeper network: same epochs, same learning rate, same seed as Exercise 3
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
deep = MLP(DEEP, output="softmax", rng=rng)
deep_history = deep.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=EPOCHS, learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE)

print("=== A - deeper network (seed 42) ===")
print(f"architecture {DEEP} (tanh hidden layers, softmax output), {deep.n_parameters} parameters; "
      f"learning rate {LEARNING_RATE}; {EPOCHS} epochs of full-batch GD")
print(f"final training loss {deep_history[-1]:.4f}; train accuracy {deep.accuracy(X_train, y_train):.2%}; "
      f"TEST ACCURACY {deep.accuracy(X_test, y_test):.2%}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# B - Controlled comparison over 10 seeds (Figure 6)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
MODELS = {"Exercise 3": SHALLOW, "Exercise 4": DEEP, "Control": WIDE}
runs = {name: [] for name in MODELS}
for name, sizes in MODELS.items():
    for seed in SEEDS:
        model = MLP(sizes, output="softmax", rng=np.random.default_rng(seed))
        history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=EPOCHS, learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE)
        C = confusion_matrix(y_test, model.predict(X_test))
        confused = {(a, b): C[a, b] + C[b, a] for a, b in [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2)]}
        runs[name].append(dict(history=history, parameters=model.n_parameters,
                               train_loss=history[-1], test_loss=model.loss(X_test, y_test),
                               train_acc=model.accuracy(X_train, y_train), test_acc=model.accuracy(X_test, y_test),
                               most_confused=max(confused, key=confused.get)))

# Seed 42 of the comparison is item A's run: same seed, same code, so the same numbers.
assert np.allclose(runs["Exercise 4"][0]["history"], deep_history)


def column(name, key):
    return np.array([run[key] for run in runs[name]])


print("\n=== B - comparison over seeds", SEEDS, "===")
print("per seed: test accuracy (Exercise 3 | Exercise 4 | control), final training loss (Exercise 3 | Exercise 4)")
for i, seed in enumerate(SEEDS):
    print(f"  seed {seed}: {column('Exercise 3', 'test_acc')[i]:.2%} | {column('Exercise 4', 'test_acc')[i]:.2%} | "

docs.title: C — Analysis
docs.text:
What was measured: the second hidden layer does not help.

  • On average the deeper network is 0.70 points worse on the test set (83.93% against 84.63%), and it wins in only 4 of 10 seeds.
  • The difference is smaller than the spread between seeds (1.45 and 1.97 points), and one test sample is worth 0.33 points, so "no gain, possibly a small loss" is the honest reading.
  • Seed 42 alone would have suggested the opposite: 85.67% against 84.67%, a one-point win. That is exactly the luck that averaging over seeds is there to remove.

The training loss and the test accuracy tell different stories.

Mean over 10 seeds Exercise 3 Exercise 4 Final training loss 0.2595 0.1661 Train accuracy 90.62% 93.88% Test accuracy 84.63% 83.93% Test loss 0.3723 0.4878 Train − test accuracy gap 5.98 points 9.95 points

The deeper network wins everywhere on the training set. Its loss is lower from the very first epochs (0.4049 against 0.4725 at epoch 100) and ends 36% lower. On the test set it is no better in accuracy and clearly worse in loss: it is more confident and no more correct. The extra capacity went into fitting the training sample, including:

  • the overlaps between adjacent clusters;
  • the 9 flipped labels in the training set;

and none of it went into structure that carries over to new data.

Why: the data does not need depth.

  • The data is 6 clusters, each a single Gaussian blob, and the boundaries that matter are between pairs of overlapping blobs. For Gaussians those boundaries are smooth (quadratic) surfaces, with no hierarchy or repetition for a second layer to exploit.
  • One layer of 16 tanh units already gives each cluster its own region (item 3D).
  • What separates the network from the oracle (84.6% against 89.3%) is not capacity. Neither more parameters (the 403-parameter control: 84.73%) nor more depth (83.93%) closes that gap.
  • The remaining errors are set by the overlap of the clouds (Figure 5b), the flipped labels, and how well 1200 samples can pin down six elongated 4-D shapes.

What depth adds, and what it costs.

  • Representationally. A second layer computes features of features: it combines the first layer's 16 soft hyperplanes into 16 new non-linear features. For a fixed number of units, this can carve out far more separate regions than a single layer. That is useful when the boundary is compositional, and irrelevant for six blobs.
  • In optimization, the cost is measurable here:
    • Instability at the same step size. With \(\eta = 0.5\), the training loss of the shallow network decreased in every one of the 2000 epochs for all 10 seeds. The loss of the deeper network went up in 16 to 812 epochs, depending on the seed, with one-epoch jumps of up to ×1.42: these are the spikes of Figure 6. Multiplying two weight matrices makes the loss surface sharper, so the same step overshoots where the shallow network's does not.
    • More dependence on the initial weights. The test accuracy varies more across seeds: ±1.97 against ±1.45 points.
    • Variance from three times the parameters, which shows in the 9.95-point train–test gap.
  • Depth against parameter count. At an equal 403 parameters, the wide one-layer control reaches 84.73% ± 0.93%. The deeper network loses to it by 0.80 points and wins in only 4 of 10 seeds. Depth is not a better way to spend the same parameters on this data.

What data would make the extra depth pay off. Depth pays when the decision boundary is compositional, that is, built by reusing simpler pieces, and when there is enough data to fit the extra parameters. Examples:

  • Parity and high-frequency patterns. In n-bit parity, a checkerboard, or nested spirals, the number of regions grows exponentially. A single layer needs exponentially many units, while a deep network can build the pattern by composition.
  • Natural signals. Images, audio and text have hierarchical features: edges combine into textures, textures into parts, and parts into objects.
  • Larger datasets. With many samples, the variance cost seen here shrinks.

Six Gaussian blobs and 1200 samples have none of these properties, so a second layer is pure cost.

docs.title: Perceptron — Understanding Perceptrons and Their Limitations
docs.text:
Luca Santana Feltrin — Insper, ANN & Deep Learning 2026.2

The thread running through this activity is separability. The same perceptron is trained on two datasets: one it was designed for, where a straight line with zero errors exists, and one where no such line exists. The interesting part is not that the second one fails. It is how it fails. The update rule keeps firing forever, and the weights the loop happens to hold when it is stopped are an arbitrary snapshot of a cycle, not an approximation of the best line.

docs.title: How to reproduce
docs.text:
Each exercise is a standalone script under code/, and both import the same model from perceptron.py. Each script opens with rng = np.random.default_rng(42) and draws everything from that single generator, from the data to the initial weights. Running a script twice therefore gives exactly the numbers reported below. Every script prints all of its reported values to stdout and rewrites its figures.

python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt --upgrade

python docs/exercises/perceptron/code/exercise1_separable.py      # ~1 s
python docs/exercises/perceptron/code/exercise2_overlapping.py    # ~10 s (includes the checks of item D)

Libraries used: numpy and matplotlib only. No third-party model is used anywhere. The activation, the prediction, the update rule and the training loop are all in perceptron.py.

docs.title: Implementation approach and challenges
docs.text:
The code is split into three files:

  • perceptron.py holds the model and nothing else:
    • step, the Heaviside activation, with \(\text{step}(0) = 1\).
    • A Perceptron class with predict, update (one sample, the \(\{0,1\}\) error-driven rule) and fit, the training loop with the stopping rule.
    • fit records the accuracy, the number of updates split by class, and \((\mathbf{w}, b)\) at the end of every epoch.
    • The pocket of Exercise 2 is part of fit from the start: after every update, if the accuracy on the full dataset beats every accuracy seen so far, \((\mathbf{w}, b)\) is copied aside. In Exercise 1 this changes nothing, since the pocket simply ends equal to the converged weights. This is what allows Exercise 2 to reuse the implementation unchanged.
  • common.py holds the data generator, the plotting helpers, and a replay of a single epoch. The replay is described in the last decision below.
  • exercise1_separable.py and exercise2_overlapping.py hold one script per exercise.

These are the decisions that took some thought, stated here because the results depend on them:

  1. Sample order. The statement does not ask for shuffling. The data is presented in generation order in every epoch: the 1000 samples of class 0, then the 1000 of class 1. This turns out to decide which wrong answer the final weights give in Exercise 2, so item 2D explains it and repeats the training with shuffled orders to check that the conclusion does not depend on it.
  2. "Changing nothing else." The \(\eta = 1.0\) re-run of item 1D must differ from the first run only in \(\eta\). \(\mathbf{w}_0\) is therefore drawn once and reused. Drawing it again from the generator would have changed two things at once.
  3. Counting epochs. The loop stops at the first full pass without an update. That pass is counted, so "26 epochs" means updates happened in epochs 1–25 and epoch 26 confirmed that none were left.
  4. Looking inside an epoch. fit only records end-of-epoch states, but the analysis of Exercise 2 needs to know what happens during an epoch. replay_epoch re-runs an epoch from the state fit recorded at the end of the previous one, using the same Perceptron.update. Because the loop is deterministic, the replay reproduces fit exactly, and the script asserts this for every epoch.

docs.title: B — Implement the perceptron
docs.text:
The model is written once, in perceptron.py, and imported unchanged by both exercises:

  • Prediction. \(\hat y = \text{step}(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b)\), with \(\text{step}(z) = 1\) if \(z \ge 0\) and \(0\) otherwise.
  • Update rule. For each sample: \(\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \eta\,(y - \hat y)\,\mathbf{x}\) and \(b \leftarrow b + \eta\,(y - \hat y)\).
    • With 0/1 labels the error \(y - \hat y\) is \(0\) on a correct prediction, so correct samples leave the weights untouched.
    • It is \(+1\) on a false negative, which pulls the line towards \(\mathbf{x}\).
    • It is \(-1\) on a false positive, which pushes the line away from it.
  • Initialization. \(\mathbf{w}_0\) is drawn from rng.normal(0, 0.01, size=2), which gives \(\mathbf{w}_0 = [0.0025, 0.0090]\) with \(\lVert\mathbf{w}_0\rVert = 0.0093\), and \(b_0 = 0\). The initial weights classify 50.35% of the points correctly, which is no better than chance.
  • Learning rate. \(\eta = 0.01\).
  • Stopping rule. The loop stops at the first full pass with no update, or after 100 epochs. The accuracy on the full dataset is recorded after every epoch.
perceptron.py
"""Single-layer perceptron, written from scratch with NumPy only.

This one implementation is imported, unchanged, by both exercises:

    exercise1_separable.py    separable data   -> the loop stops on its own
    exercise2_overlapping.py  overlapping data -> the loop never stops; the pocket keeps the best weights

Labels are 0/1, so the update rule is the error-driven one

    w <- w + eta * (y - y_hat) * x,        b <- b + eta * (y - y_hat),

whose error (y - y_hat) is 0 on a correct prediction and +1 / -1 on the two kinds of mistake.
(The textbook form w <- w + eta * y * x belongs to -1/+1 labels: with 0/1 labels it would never
update on class 0, so a false positive could never be corrected.)
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

import numpy as np


def step(z):
    """Heaviside step: 1 where z >= 0, 0 otherwise. Works on scalars and arrays alike."""
    return np.where(z >= 0, 1, 0)


@dataclass
class History:
    """What `Perceptron.fit` records, one entry per epoch (a full pass over the data)."""

    accuracy: list = field(default_factory=list)        # accuracy of the current weights at the end of the epoch
    best_accuracy: list = field(default_factory=list)   # pocket (best-so-far) accuracy at the end of the epoch
    updates: list = field(default_factory=list)         # number of updates in the epoch, as (on class 0, on class 1)
    w: list = field(default_factory=list)               # weights at the end of the epoch
    b: list = field(default_factory=list)               # bias at the end of the epoch
    converged: bool = False                             # True if some epoch finished without a single update

    @property
    def epochs(self) -> int:
        """Number of epochs run, including the final update-free one when the loop converged."""
        return len(self.accuracy)


class Perceptron:
    """Perceptron y_hat = step(w . x + b), trained sample by sample with the 0/1 error-driven rule."""

    def __init__(self, w0, b0: float = 0.0, eta: float = 0.01):
        self.w = np.array(w0, dtype=float)  # copied, so the caller's w0 is never modified
        self.b = float(b0)
        self.eta = eta

        # Pocket: the best weights seen so far. Filled by `fit`, which starts it at the initial weights.
        self.pocket_w = self.w.copy()
        self.pocket_b = self.b
        self.pocket_accuracy = -np.inf
        self.pocket_epoch = 0

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ prediction
    def net_input(self, X):
        """w . x + b for every row of X (or for a single sample)."""
        return X @ self.w + self.b

    def predict(self, X):
        """y_hat = step(w . x + b)."""
        return step(self.net_input(X))

    def accuracy(self, X, y) -> float:
        """Fraction of samples whose prediction matches the label."""
        return float(np.mean(self.predict(X) == y))

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ learning
    def update(self, x, y) -> int:
        """Present one sample: predict it, apply the update rule and return the error (y - y_hat).

        A correct prediction gives error 0, so the weights are left untouched.
        """
        error = int(y - self.predict(x))
        if error != 0:
            self.w += self.eta * error * x
            self.b += self.eta * error
        return error

    def fit(self, X, y, max_epochs: int = 100) -> History:
        """Train until a full pass produces no update, or for `max_epochs` passes, whichever comes first.

        The samples are presented in the order they are stored in X, every epoch.
        """
        history = History()

        # The initial weights are the first ones "seen", so they seed the pocket.
        self.pocket_w, self.pocket_b = self.w.copy(), self.b
        self.pocket_accuracy, self.pocket_epoch = self.accuracy(X, y), 0

        for epoch in range(1, max_epochs + 1):
            updates = [0, 0]  # updates triggered by class-0 and by class-1 samples in this epoch
            for x_i, y_i in zip(X, y):
                if self.update(x_i, y_i) != 0:
                    updates[y_i] += 1
                    # Pocket algorithm - the only addition to the plain perceptron loop: after every
                    # update, if the new weights beat every accuracy seen so far, copy them aside.
                    acc = self.accuracy(X, y)
                    if acc > self.pocket_accuracy:
                        self.pocket_w, self.pocket_b = self.w.copy(), self.b
                        self.pocket_accuracy, self.pocket_epoch = acc, epoch

            history.accuracy.append(self.accuracy(X, y))
            history.best_accuracy.append(self.pocket_accuracy)
            history.updates.append(tuple(updates))
            history.w.append(self.w.copy())
            history.b.append(self.b)

            # Stopping rule: an epoch without a single update means every sample is classified
            # correctly, so the weights can no longer change.
            if sum(updates) == 0:
                history.converged = True
                break

        return history

docs.title: D — Analysis
docs.text:
Why does separable data converge quickly?

The update rule is error-driven: \(y - \hat y = 0\) on every correctly classified sample, so only mistakes move the weights. On separable data there is at least one line that makes no mistakes. The perceptron convergence theorem guarantees that the loop reaches such a line after a finite number of mistakes, at most \((R/\gamma)^2\), a bound that depends on the geometry of the data and not on how many samples or epochs there are. Once the loop gets there, every error is zero, the weights stop moving, and the stopping rule fires. Convergence is exact, not approximate.

The numbers show how little work that takes:

  • 73 updates in total (49 on class 0, 24 on class 1) over 52 000 sample presentations. 99.86% of the presentations changed nothing.
  • The updates per epoch are few from the very start: 2 to 4 per epoch, i.e. at most 0.2% of the 2000 samples.
  • The count drops to 1 in epoch 25 and to 0 in epoch 26, and there the loop stops by itself.
  • Only 14 distinct samples ever triggered an update, and 27 of the 73 updates were on the very first sample of a class block.

Figure 3 also shows why it takes 26 epochs rather than 2. The accuracy zig-zags between 50% and 95% because the weights start tiny (0.0093), while one mistake moves them a lot:

  • Each mistake moves \(\mathbf{w}\) by \(\eta\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert \approx 0.047\) and \(b\) by only \(\eta = 0.01\).
  • The first class-0 samples of an epoch push the line one way, and the first class-1 sample pushes it back.
  • To sit in the gap, the line needs an offset of \(-b/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert \approx 4.3\) from the origin (the midpoint of the class means along \(\mathbf{w}\) is at 4.43), so \(b\) has to become several times \(\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert\).
  • But \(b\) changes by exactly \(\pm\eta\) per mistake, so \(b = \eta\,(N_1 - N_0) = 0.01 \cdot (24 - 49) = \mathbf{-0.25}\). That is 25 net class-0 corrections, about one per epoch, which is the 25 epochs with updates.

The mistakes that remain are few, and each one is a correction towards a line that exists. What sets the number of epochs is how slowly the bias can walk.

The same training with \(\eta = 1.0\). Same data, same order, same \(\mathbf{w}_0\):

Run Epochs Accuracy \(\mathbf{w}\) \(b\) \(\mathbf{w}/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert\) Angle of \(\mathbf{w}\) Offset \(-b/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert\) \(\eta = 0.01\) 26 100.00% [0.0505, 0.0289] −0.25 [0.8681, 0.4963] 29.759° 4.2979 \(\eta = 1.0\) 37 100.00% [5.8706, 3.3592] −31.00 [0.8679, 0.4967] 29.779° 4.5832

Both runs separate the data perfectly, but with different boundaries (Figure 2b). Here the two directions agree to within 0.02°, so the lines are practically parallel. The difference is where they sit along that direction: 4.30 against 4.58 from the origin, a gap of 0.29. The runs also take different numbers of epochs, 26 against 37.

Figure 2b — the boundaries learned with \(\eta = 0.01\) (solid) and \(\eta = 1.0\) (dashed) from the same \(\mathbf{w}_0\), zoomed on the gap between the classes.

What \(\eta\) controls. Unrolling the rule gives \(\mathbf{w}_T = \mathbf{w}_0 + \eta\sum_t e_t\,\mathbf{x}_t\) and \(b_T = \eta\sum_t e_t\), where \(e_t = y_t - \hat y_t\). Dividing by \(\eta > 0\) does not change any prediction, because step only reads a sign. So the run \((\mathbf{w}_0, \eta)\) makes exactly the same mistakes as a run with \(\eta = 1\) started from \(\mathbf{w}_0/\eta\). The only thing \(\eta\) changes is how large the random start is compared with one update, and a single update adds \(\mathbf{x}\), with \(\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert \approx 4.65\) on average:

  • \(\eta = 0.01\) behaves like a start of size \(\lVert\mathbf{w}_0\rVert/\eta = 0.93\), about a fifth of one update. That is enough to tilt the first predictions and change which samples are misclassified early on. The sequence of mistakes then differs, with 25 net bias steps instead of 31, so the line ends at a different offset.
  • \(\eta = 1.0\) behaves like a start of size 0.0093, 1/500 of one update. The random start is wiped out by the first mistake, and the run is the zero-start run. Its weights differ from the \(\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}\), \(\eta = 1\) run by exactly \([0.0025, 0.0090] = \mathbf{w}_0\), with the same \(b = -31\) and the same 37 epochs: it made exactly the same mistakes.

What would have happened from \(\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}\), \(b = 0\). Write \((\mathbf{w}^{(\eta)}_t, b^{(\eta)}_t)\) for the state after \(t\) sample presentations with learning rate \(\eta\), starting from zero. Let \((\mathbf{u}_t, c_t)\) be the same run with \(\eta = 1\).

Claim: \(\mathbf{w}^{(\eta)}_t = \eta\,\mathbf{u}_t\) and \(b^{(\eta)}_t = \eta\,c_t\) for every \(t\) and every \(\eta > 0\).

Proof by induction.

  • Base. At \(t = 0\), \(\mathbf{0} = \eta\cdot\mathbf{0}\) and \(0 = \eta\cdot 0\).
  • Step. Assume the claim holds at \(t\), and let \((\mathbf{x}, y)\) be the next sample. The prediction is [ \hat y^{(\eta)} = \text{step}\big(\eta(\mathbf{u}t\cdot\mathbf{x} + c_t)\big) = \text{step}\big(\mathbf{u}t\cdot\mathbf{x} + c_t\big) = \hat y^{(1)}, ] because multiplying by \(\eta > 0\) keeps the sign of a non-zero number and keeps zero at zero, so \(\text{step}\) returns the same value. The error \(e = y - \hat y\) is therefore the same in both runs, and [ \mathbf{w}^{(\eta)}} = \eta\,\mathbf{ut + \eta\,e\,\mathbf{x} = \eta\,(\mathbf{u}t + e\,\mathbf{x}) = \eta\,\mathbf{u}, \qquad b^{(\eta)} = \eta\,c_t + \eta\,e = \eta\,c. \qquad\blacksquare ]

Applying the claim to two learning rates gives \(\mathbf{w}^{(\eta_2)}_t = (\eta_2/\eta_1)\,\mathbf{w}^{(\eta_1)}_t\) and \(b^{(\eta_2)}_t = (\eta_2/\eta_1)\,b^{(\eta_1)}_t\) at every step. Two consequences follow:

  • The same predictions at every step. Both runs make the same mistakes and reach their first update-free pass in the same epoch, so the epoch count is identical.
  • The same boundary. The set \(\{\mathbf{x} : \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b = 0\}\) does not change when \((\mathbf{w}, b)\) is multiplied by a positive constant.

So from a zero start \(\eta\) has no effect at all. The script checks this numerically:

Zero start \(\mathbf{w}\) \(b\) Epochs Accuracy \(\eta = 0.01\) [0.0587, 0.0335] −0.31 37 100.00% \(\eta = 1.0\) [5.8681, 3.3503] −31.00 37 100.00%

The ratio is exactly 100 in \(\mathbf{w}\) and in \(b\), at the end of every one of the 37 epochs, and the two runs give identical predictions on all 2000 points. With \(\mathbf{w}_0 \ne \mathbf{0}\) the base case fails: \(\mathbf{w}_0\) is not \(\eta\) times anything independent of \(\eta\). That is the only reason the two runs of the previous paragraph could differ, and it is why item B forbids the zero start.

"""Shared by both exercises: the seed, the data generator, the plotting helpers and an epoch replay.

The perceptron itself lives in perceptron.py; nothing here learns anything.
"""

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

from perceptron import Perceptron

# One seed for the whole report: every script builds rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED).
SEED = 42

FIGURES = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "figures"
FIGURES.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

COLORS = ["#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e"]  # class 0, class 1


def generate_two_classes(rng, mean0, mean1, cov, n_per_class=1000):
    """Draw `n_per_class` 2D points per class from multivariate normals sharing the covariance `cov`.

    The data is returned in generation order - all of class 0, then all of class 1 - and is
    never shuffled, so the perceptron sees the samples in exactly this order in every epoch.
    """
    X0 = rng.multivariate_normal(mean0, cov, size=n_per_class)
    X1 = rng.multivariate_normal(mean1, cov, size=n_per_class)
    X = np.vstack([X0, X1])
    y = np.concatenate([np.zeros(n_per_class, dtype=int), np.ones(n_per_class, dtype=int)])
    return X, y


def scatter_classes(ax, X, y, *, s=12, alpha=0.55):
    """Scatter the two classes on `ax`, one colour each."""
    for k in (0, 1):
        cloud = X[y == k]
        ax.scatter(cloud[:, 0], cloud[:, 1], s=s, alpha=alpha, color=COLORS[k],
                   label=f"Class {k} ({len(cloud)} points)")
    ax.set_xlabel("Feature 1 ($x_1$)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Feature 2 ($x_2$)")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25, linestyle=":")


def mark_misclassified(ax, X, wrong, label="Misclassified"):
    """Circle the points flagged in the boolean mask `wrong` (the legend shows how many)."""
    ax.scatter(X[wrong, 0], X[wrong, 1], s=46, facecolors="none", edgecolors="black",
               linewidths=0.9, label=f"{label} ({int(wrong.sum())})")


def draw_boundary(ax, w, b, **kwargs):
    """Draw the line w . x + b = 0 across the current axis limits, without changing them."""
    xlim, ylim = ax.get_xlim(), ax.get_ylim()
    if abs(w[1]) >= abs(w[0]):  # closer to horizontal: solve for x2
        x1 = np.linspace(*xlim, 400)
        ax.plot(x1, -(w[0] * x1 + b) / w[1], **kwargs)
    else:                       # closer to vertical: solve for x1
        x2 = np.linspace(*ylim, 400)
        ax.plot(-(w[1] * x2 + b) / w[0], x2, **kwargs)
    ax.set_xlim(xlim)
    ax.set_ylim(ylim)


def boundary_offset(w, b) -> float:
    """Signed distance from the origin to the line w . x + b = 0, measured along w."""
    return float(-b / np.linalg.norm(w))


def angle_deg(w) -> float:
    """Angle of the weight vector w with the x1 axis, in degrees."""
    return float(np.degrees(np.arctan2(w[1], w[0])))


def replay_epoch(w, b, eta, X, y):
    """Re-run one epoch from (w, b) with Perceptron.update, to see *where* in the epoch things happen.

    `fit` only records the end of each epoch; replaying the epoch from the (w, b) stored at the end of
    the previous one reproduces it exactly (the loop is deterministic) and exposes the inside of it.

    Returns the indices of the samples that triggered an update, the (w, b) held right after the
    class-0 block (first half of the epoch) and the (w, b) at the end of the epoch.
    """
    model = Perceptron(w, b, eta)
    n_class0 = int(np.sum(y == 0))
    mistakes, after_class0 = [], None
    for i, (x_i, y_i) in enumerate(zip(X, y)):
        if i == n_class0:
            after_class0 = (model.w.copy(), model.b)
        if model.update(x_i, y_i) != 0:
            mistakes.append(i)
    return mistakes, after_class0, (model.w.copy(), model.b)


def replay_training(w0, b0, eta, X, y, history):
    """Replay every epoch of a finished `fit`, starting each one from the state stored by `fit`.

    Also checks that each replayed epoch ends exactly where `fit` recorded it did.
    """
    starts = [(np.asarray(w0, dtype=float), float(b0))] + list(zip(history.w, history.b))[:-1]
    epochs = []
    for (w_start, b_start), w_end, b_end in zip(starts, history.w, history.b):
        mistakes, after_class0, end = replay_epoch(w_start, b_start, eta, X, y)
        assert np.allclose(end[0], w_end) and np.isclose(end[1], b_end), "replay diverged from fit"
        epochs.append((mistakes, after_class0, end))
    return epochs

"""Exercise 1 - Separable data: the case the perceptron was designed for.

Generates two well-separated Gaussian classes, trains the perceptron of perceptron.py on them,
repeats the training with eta = 1.0 from the same starting weights, checks that from a zero
start eta only rescales the weights, and writes Figures 1, 2, 2b and 3.

Every number quoted in the report is printed by this script. Run it from the repository root:

    python docs/exercises/perceptron/code/exercise1_separable.py
"""

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")  # no interactive display needed: we only save files
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.ticker import MaxNLocator

from common import (COLORS, FIGURES, SEED, angle_deg, boundary_offset, draw_boundary,
                    generate_two_classes, mark_misclassified, replay_training, scatter_classes)
from perceptron import Perceptron

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Setup: one seed, one generator, used for everything below
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

# Generating parameters given in the statement
MEAN_0 = [1.5, 1.5]
MEAN_1 = [5.0, 5.0]
COV = [[0.5, 0.0], [0.0, 0.5]]
N_PER_CLASS = 1000

ETA = 0.01          # learning rate of items B and C
ETA_LARGE = 1.0     # learning rate of the re-run in item D
MAX_EPOCHS = 100

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A - Generate the data (Figure 1)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
X, y = generate_two_classes(rng, MEAN_0, MEAN_1, COV, N_PER_CLASS)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6.5))
scatter_classes(ax, X, y)
ax.set_title("Figure 1 - Exercise 1 data: two separable Gaussian classes (2000 points)")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", framealpha=0.95)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIGURES / "fig1_data.png", dpi=150)
plt.close(fig)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# B - The perceptron (perceptron.py) and its initial weights
# w0 is drawn ONCE and reused by the eta = 1.0 run of item D, which must change nothing but eta.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
w0 = rng.normal(0, 0.01, size=2)
initial_accuracy = Perceptron(w0, 0.0, ETA).accuracy(X, y)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# C - Train and measure (Figures 2 and 3)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
model = Perceptron(w0, b0=0.0, eta=ETA)
history = model.fit(X, y, max_epochs=MAX_EPOCHS)
wrong = model.predict(X) != y

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6.5))
scatter_classes(ax, X, y)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
draw_boundary(ax, model.w, model.b, color="black", linewidth=2,
              label=r"Decision boundary $\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b = 0$")
mark_misclassified(ax, X, wrong)
ax.set_title(f"Figure 2 - Perceptron decision boundary ($\\eta = {ETA}$, "
             f"{history.epochs} epochs, accuracy {model.accuracy(X, y):.2%})")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", framealpha=0.95)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIGURES / "fig2_boundary.png", dpi=150)
plt.close(fig)

epochs = np.arange(0, history.epochs + 1)
accuracy_curve = [initial_accuracy] + history.accuracy          # epoch 0 = initial weights
updates = np.array(history.updates)                             # (epochs, 2): class 0, class 1

fig, (ax_acc, ax_upd) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 7.5), sharex=True,
                                     gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [3, 2]})
ax_acc.plot(epochs, np.array(accuracy_curve) * 100, marker="o", markersize=4, color="black",
            label="Accuracy on the full dataset (end of epoch)")
ax_acc.axhline(100, color="grey", linestyle=":", linewidth=1, label="100%")
ax_acc.set_ylabel("Accuracy (%)")
ax_acc.set_title(f"Figure 3 - Accuracy $\\times$ epoch ($\\eta = {ETA}$); epoch 0 = initial weights")
ax_acc.grid(alpha=0.25, linestyle=":")
ax_acc.legend(loc="lower right")
ax_upd.bar(epochs[1:], updates[:, 0], color=COLORS[0], label="Updates triggered by class 0")
ax_upd.bar(epochs[1:], updates[:, 1], bottom=updates[:, 0], color=COLORS[1],
           label="Updates triggered by class 1")
ax_upd.set_xlabel("Epoch")
ax_upd.set_ylabel("Updates in the epoch")
ax_upd.yaxis.set_major_locator(MaxNLocator(integer=True))
ax_upd.grid(alpha=0.25, linestyle=":")
ax_upd.legend(loc="upper right")
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIGURES / "fig3_accuracy.png", dpi=150)
plt.close(fig)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# D - Analysis: where in the epoch the updates happen, and how far the bias has to walk
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
replayed = replay_training(w0, 0.0, ETA, X, y, history)
mistake_positions = [i for mistakes, _, _ in replayed for i in mistakes]
block_starts = {0, N_PER_CLASS}                              # first sample of each class block
n_on_block_start = sum(i in block_starts for i in mistake_positions)
# Every update moves b by exactly +eta (class-1 mistake) or -eta (class-0 mistake), so
# b_final = b0 + eta * (updates on class 1 - updates on class 0).
b_walk = ETA * (updates[:, 1].sum() - updates[:, 0].sum())

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# D - Analysis: the same training with eta = 1.0, and the zero start
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
model_large = Perceptron(w0, b0=0.0, eta=ETA_LARGE)       # same w0, same b0, same data order
history_large = model_large.fit(X, y, max_epochs=MAX_EPOCHS)

direction = model.w / np.linalg.norm(model.w)
direction_large = model_large.w / np.linalg.norm(model_large.w)
angle_between = float(np.degrees(np.arccos(np.clip(direction @ direction_large, -1, 1))))

# From w = 0, b = 0 the claim is that eta only rescales the whole trajectory.
zero_small = Perceptron(np.zeros(2), 0.0, ETA)
zero_large = Perceptron(np.zeros(2), 0.0, ETA_LARGE)
history_zero_small = zero_small.fit(X, y, max_epochs=MAX_EPOCHS)
history_zero_large = zero_large.fit(X, y, max_epochs=MAX_EPOCHS)
ratio = ETA_LARGE / ETA
same_trajectory = all(
    np.allclose(w_l, ratio * w_s) and np.isclose(b_l, ratio * b_s)
    for w_s, w_l, b_s, b_l in zip(history_zero_small.w, history_zero_large.w,
                                  history_zero_small.b, history_zero_large.b)
)

# Figure 2b: both learned boundaries, zoomed on the gap between the classes
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6.5))
scatter_classes(ax, X, y)
ax.set_xlim(0.5, 6.0)
ax.set_ylim(0.5, 6.0)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
draw_boundary(ax, model.w, model.b, color="black", linewidth=2,
              label=f"$\\eta = {ETA}$: {history.epochs} epochs")
draw_boundary(ax, model_large.w, model_large.b, color="#d62728", linewidth=2, linestyle="--",
              label=f"$\\eta = {ETA_LARGE}$: {history_large.epochs} epochs")
ax.set_title("Figure 2b - Both learned boundaries, same data and same $\\mathbf{w}_0$ (zoom on the gap)")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", framealpha=0.95)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIGURES / "fig2b_eta_boundaries.png", dpi=150)
plt.close(fig)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reported numbers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    np.set_printoptions(precision=4, suppress=True)
    norms = np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1)

    print("=" * 78)
    print("EXERCISE 1 - SEPARABLE DATA")
    print(f"seed = {SEED} | 2 classes x {N_PER_CLASS} samples | order: all class 0, then all class 1")
    print("=" * 78)

    print("\n[A] generating parameters and sample statistics")
    for k, mean in enumerate((MEAN_0, MEAN_1)):
        cloud = X[y == k]
        print(f"  class {k}: mean={mean} cov={COV} | sample mean={cloud.mean(axis=0)}"
              f" sample std={cloud.std(axis=0)}")
    print(f"  ||x|| over the dataset: mean {norms.mean():.4f}, min {norms.min():.4f}, max {norms.max():.4f}")

    print("\n[B] initialisation")
    print(f"  w0 = {w0}  (||w0|| = {np.linalg.norm(w0):.5f}),  b0 = 0.0")
    print(f"  accuracy of the initial weights = {initial_accuracy:.4f}")

    print(f"\n[C] training with eta = {ETA}")
    print(f"  final w = {model.w},  final b = {model.b:.4f}")
    print(f"  epochs = {history.epochs} (converged = {history.converged}; "
          f"last update in epoch {history.epochs - 1}, epoch {history.epochs} is the update-free pass)")
    print(f"  final accuracy = {model.accuracy(X, y):.4f}  ({int(wrong.sum())} misclassified)")
    print(f"  accuracy per epoch = {np.round(history.accuracy, 4).tolist()}")

    print("\n[D] updates per epoch (class 0, class 1) and ||w|| at the end of each epoch")
    for e, ((u0, u1), w_e) in enumerate(zip(history.updates, history.w), start=1):
        print(f"  epoch {e:>2}: {u0} + {u1} = {u0 + u1} updates | ||w|| = {np.linalg.norm(w_e):.4f}")
    print(f"  total updates = {int(updates.sum())} "
          f"(class 0: {int(updates[:, 0].sum())}, class 1: {int(updates[:, 1].sum())}) "
          f"over {history.epochs * len(X)} sample presentations "
          f"({1 - updates.sum() / (history.epochs * len(X)):.2%} of the presentations change nothing)")
    print(f"  samples that ever triggered an update: {sorted(set(mistake_positions))}")
    print(f"  updates triggered by the FIRST sample of a class block (index 0 or {N_PER_CLASS}): "
          f"{n_on_block_start} of {len(mistake_positions)}")
    print(f"  bias walk: eta * (class-1 updates - class-0 updates) = {b_walk:.4f} = final b ({model.b:.4f})")
    print(f"  per mistake: |delta b| = eta = {ETA}, ||delta w|| = eta * ||x|| = {ETA * norms.mean():.4f} on average")
    print(f"  offset the boundary needs, -b/||w||, at the end = {boundary_offset(model.w, model.b):.4f} "
          f"(midpoint of the class means along w: "
          f"{float(((np.array(MEAN_0) + np.array(MEAN_1)) / 2) @ model.w / np.linalg.norm(model.w)):.4f})")

    print(f"\n[D] eta = {ETA} against eta = {ETA_LARGE} (same data, same w0, same order)")
    for name, m, h in (("eta=0.01", model, history), ("eta=1.0 ", model_large, history_large)):
        d = m.w / np.linalg.norm(m.w)
        print(f"  {name}: w = {m.w}, b = {m.b:.4f}, epochs = {h.epochs}, accuracy = {m.accuracy(X, y):.4f}"
              f" | w/||w|| = {d}, angle = {angle_deg(m.w):.3f} deg,"
              f" boundary offset -b/||w|| = {boundary_offset(m.w, m.b):.4f}")
    print(f"  angle between the two directions = {angle_between:.4f} deg")

    print(f"  ||w0|| / eta: eta=0.01 -> {np.linalg.norm(w0) / ETA:.4f}, "

    print("\n[D] zero start w = 0, b = 0")

    for name in ("fig1_data.png", "fig2_boundary.png", "fig2b_eta_boundaries.png", "fig3_accuracy.png"):

docs.title: B — Train, keeping the best weights
docs.text:
The run uses the Exercise 1 implementation, unchanged, with \(\eta = 0.01\), a cap of 100 epochs, the same kind of initialization (\(\mathbf{w}_0 = [0.0025, 0.0090]\), \(b_0 = 0\)) and the pocket tracked inside fit. The loop never stops on its own: all 100 epochs run, and even the quietest epoch had 2 updates.

Weights \(\mathbf{w}\) \(b\) Accuracy Misclassified Final (after epoch 100) [0.0361, 0.0494] −0.0400 50.05% 999 Pocket (best seen, epoch 18) [0.0068, 0.0066] −0.0500 72.85% 543 Reference, not fitted: Bayes line \(x_1 + x_2 = 7\) [1, 1] −7 72.60% (71.81% expected) 548

The reference row is the Bayes-optimal boundary for two Gaussians with equal covariance: the perpendicular bisector of the means. On this sample it scores 72.60%, and its expected accuracy is \(\Phi(\sqrt2 / (2\sqrt{1.5})) = 71.81\%\). The pocket is right on it, slightly above because it was picked on the sample itself. The final weights are at chance.
