docs.title: D — Analysis
docs.text:
Explain the gap. Where does the final boundary sit, and why does the loop leave it there?

The final line sits outside the cloud. Its offset from the origin is \(-b/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert = 0.65\), while the centre of the data lies 4.86 from the origin along the same direction. The line therefore runs below and to the left of all the data (Figure 5, left), and 99.95% of the points fall on its positive side. The final weights predict class 1 for almost everything, which misclassifies 999 points (the whole of class 0 minus one) and scores 50.05%, the share of class 1. The pocket line has offset 5.25 against a data centre at 4.92, at an angle of 44.1° against the Bayes line's 45°. It cuts through the middle of the overlap, as the best line must.

Three facts from the update rule explain why the loop leaves the line there.

  1. The bias cannot walk. Following the hint:
    • Per mistake, \(b\) moves by \(\eta = 0.01\), while \(\mathbf{w}\) moves by \(\eta\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert \approx 0.051\), about 5 times more, since \(\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert \approx 5.07\) here.
    • To pass through the centre of the cloud with the final \(\mathbf{w}\), the bias would have to be \(-0.297\). It is \(-0.04\).
    • The bias is just a count of mistakes, \(b = \eta\,(N_1 - N_0) = 0.01\cdot(189 - 193)\). Mistakes on the two classes come in pairs and cancel, so \(b\) hovers near zero.
    • \(\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert\) never grows either: it stays between 0.0088 and 0.0689 over the 100 epochs.
    • A line with \(b \approx 0\) passes near the origin, and the origin is ~5 units from a cloud that sits entirely in the first quadrant.
  2. One mistake throws the line across the whole cloud.
    • A mistake on \(\mathbf{x}\) shifts the score \(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}' + b\) of every point \(\mathbf{x}'\) by \(\eta\,e\,(\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{x}' + 1)\). All points here sit around \((3.5, 3.5)\), so \(\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{x}' \approx 24\) on average, and that shift is about 0.25.
    • The scores of the whole dataset under the final weights have a standard deviation of only 0.089.
    • A single update therefore moves every point's score by almost three standard deviations of the whole distribution. It does not nudge the line through the cloud; it pushes the line clean across it.
  3. The last mistake of every epoch is on class 1. Replaying the epochs shows the cycle:
    • The first class-0 sample is predicted 1. That mistake throws the line to the other side, and every point is now predicted 0. The remaining class-0 samples are correct and cause no updates.
    • The first class-1 sample is then predicted 0. That mistake throws the line back, and every point is predicted 1 for the rest of the epoch.
    • 200 of the 382 updates, two per epoch, were on the very first sample of a class block.
    • After the class-0 block, the model predicts class 1 for 0.00% of the points in every one of the 100 epochs. At the end of the epoch it predicts class 1 for 99.80% on average (Figure 6b).

"The final weights" are the snapshot taken at the end of the class-1 block, so they are always the "everything is class 1" half of the cycle. That is how the loop ends at ≈ 50%, and it would do so whatever the epoch cap. The pocket only works because it evaluates the accuracy after every update: once in a while (epoch 18 here), an update lands the line inside the cloud before the next mistake throws it out again, and the pocket keeps that moment.

Figure 6b — share of the 2000 points predicted as class 1, halfway through each epoch (after the class-0 block) and at its end. The weights flip between "all class 0" and "all class 1" twice per epoch. The flat red curve of Figure 6 is this oscillation, always sampled at the same phase.

Figure 3 against Figure 6. What does the convergence theorem guarantee, and which assumption is broken?

  • Figure 3. The curve reaches 100%, and in epoch 26 a full pass produces no update, so the loop stops by itself.
  • Figure 6. All 100 epochs run and no epoch is ever update-free (between 2 and 4 updates, 3.82 on average). The red curve never leaves 50.05%–52.35%, while the pocket climbs in steps to 72.85% and then stays flat. The red curve looks calm only because it is always sampled at the same point of the cycle; Figure 6b shows that the weights never settle.

The perceptron convergence theorem (Rosenblatt; Novikoff's bound) has two hypotheses:

  • The data is linearly separable with a margin: some unit vector \((\mathbf{w}^*, b^*)\) puts every point on its correct side at a distance of at least \(\gamma > 0\).
  • The inputs are bounded, \(\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert \le R\).

Under these hypotheses the perceptron makes at most \((R/\gamma)^2\) mistakes, in any order of presentation, and then stops with a separating line. This dataset breaks the first hypothesis:

  • No line separates the classes. Even the Bayes line misclassifies 27.40% of the points, so no \(\gamma > 0\) exists and the bound is void.
  • For every \((\mathbf{w}, b)\) there is always some misclassified sample, so the error-driven rule fires in every epoch, forever.
  • The theorem says nothing about the quality of the iterate once its hypothesis fails. What actually happens is the cycle above.

Does adding more epochs fix it? Does a smaller \(\eta\)?

Neither. The argument comes from the update rule:

  • More epochs. The cycle does not depend on the epoch number. Every epoch has a misclassified sample, so every epoch updates, and every epoch ends right after the class-1 flip. More epochs only replay the same cycle more times. They also give the pocket more chances to catch a good moment, but they do nothing for the final iterate.
  • Smaller \(\eta\). From the scaling argument of item 1D, the run with \(\mathbf{w}_0\) and rate \(\eta\) makes the same mistakes as a run with rate 1 started from \(\mathbf{w}_0/\eta\). A smaller \(\eta\) therefore only makes the random start relatively larger, which affects the first few epochs and nothing after that. The quantity that causes the flip does not depend on \(\eta\): the score shift per mistake and the spread of the scores both scale with \(\eta\), so their ratio (≈ 2.8 here) is the same. The ratio \(|\Delta b| / \lVert\Delta\mathbf{w}\rVert = 1/\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\) does not involve \(\eta\) at all.

The script confirms both answers. Every run below uses the same data and the same \(\mathbf{w}_0\):

\(\eta\) Epochs Final accuracy Pocket accuracy Updates in the last epoch 0.01 100 50.05% 72.85% 4 0.01 1000 50.30% 73.35% 4 0.001 100 50.10% 72.85% 4 0.001 1000 50.35% 73.15% 4

The final iterate stays at chance and the loop is still updating in the last epoch, whatever the budget and whatever the rate. Only the pocket reaches the best line.

Is the ≈ 50% an artefact of presenting the classes in two blocks? The exact number is, but the failure is not. The same training was repeated with shuffled data:

Order Final accuracy Pocket / best seen Converged Shuffled once 72.60% 73.40% No Reshuffled every epoch 57.70% 73.35% No
  • Shuffled once. The accuracy at the end of an epoch swings anywhere between 52.35% and 73.05%, and this time the last snapshot happened to land high.
  • Reshuffled every epoch. The last snapshot landed at 57.70%.
  • Neither order converges. In every order, the final weights are wherever the last mistake left them, which is a lottery. Only the pocket reliably returns the best line.

The order decides which arbitrary snapshot the final weights are; separability is what would make the snapshot stop moving.

exercise2_overlapping.py
"""Exercise 2 - Overlapping data: the case the perceptron cannot solve.

Generates two heavily overlapping Gaussian classes, trains the SAME perceptron of perceptron.py
(eta = 0.01, 100 epochs), compares the final weights with the pocket (best-so-far) weights,
measures why the final ones land where they do, and writes Figures 4, 5, 6 and 6b.

Every number quoted in the report is printed by this script. Run it from the repository root:

    python docs/exercises/perceptron/code/exercise2_overlapping.py

The checks of item D (1000 epochs, eta = 0.001, shuffled orders) take about 10 seconds in total.
"""

from math import erf, sqrt

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")  # no interactive display needed: we only save files
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from common import (FIGURES, SEED, angle_deg, boundary_offset, draw_boundary, generate_two_classes,
                    mark_misclassified, replay_training, scatter_classes)
from perceptron import Perceptron, step

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Setup: one seed, one generator, used for everything below
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

# Generating parameters given in the statement
MEAN_0 = [3.0, 3.0]
MEAN_1 = [4.0, 4.0]
COV = [[1.5, 0.0], [0.0, 1.5]]
N_PER_CLASS = 1000

ETA = 0.01
MAX_EPOCHS = 100

FINAL_STYLE = dict(color="#d62728", linewidth=2.2)                   # final weights: solid red
POCKET_STYLE = dict(color="#2ca02c", linewidth=2.2, linestyle="--")  # pocket weights: dashed green

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A - Generate the data (Figure 4)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
X, y = generate_two_classes(rng, MEAN_0, MEAN_1, COV, N_PER_CLASS)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6.5))
scatter_classes(ax, X, y, alpha=0.45)
ax.set_title("Figure 4 - Exercise 2 data: two overlapping Gaussian classes (2000 points)")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", framealpha=0.95)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIGURES / "fig4_data.png", dpi=150)
plt.close(fig)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# B - Train with the Exercise 1 implementation, unchanged; the pocket is tracked inside `fit`
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
w0 = rng.normal(0, 0.01, size=2)
initial_accuracy = Perceptron(w0, 0.0, ETA).accuracy(X, y)

model = Perceptron(w0, b0=0.0, eta=ETA)
history = model.fit(X, y, max_epochs=MAX_EPOCHS)

final_w, final_b = model.w.copy(), model.b
pocket_w, pocket_b = model.pocket_w.copy(), model.pocket_b
pocket_model = Perceptron(pocket_w, pocket_b, ETA)       # only used to predict with the pocket weights
final_accuracy = model.accuracy(X, y)
pocket_accuracy = pocket_model.accuracy(X, y)
wrong_final = model.predict(X) != y
wrong_pocket = pocket_model.predict(X) != y

# Reference only - nothing is fitted: for two Gaussians with equal covariance the Bayes-optimal
# boundary is the perpendicular bisector of the means, x1 + x2 = 7.
bayes_w, bayes_b = np.array([1.0, 1.0]), -7.0
bayes_accuracy = float(np.mean(step(X @ bayes_w + bayes_b) == y))
# Its expected accuracy is Phi(||mu1 - mu0|| / (2 sigma)) = Phi(sqrt(2) / (2 sqrt(1.5))).
separation = np.linalg.norm(np.array(MEAN_1) - np.array(MEAN_0)) / (2 * sqrt(COV[0][0]))
bayes_expected = 0.5 * (1 + erf(separation / sqrt(2)))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# C - Figures 5 and 6
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 7), sharex=True, sharey=True)
panels = (
    ("final", final_w, final_b, wrong_final, final_accuracy),
    ("pocket", pocket_w, pocket_b, wrong_pocket, pocket_accuracy),
)
for ax, (name, w, b, wrong, acc) in zip(axes, panels):
    scatter_classes(ax, X, y, s=10, alpha=0.35)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    draw_boundary(ax, final_w, final_b, label=f"Final weights ({final_accuracy:.2%})", **FINAL_STYLE)
    draw_boundary(ax, pocket_w, pocket_b, label=f"Pocket weights ({pocket_accuracy:.2%})", **POCKET_STYLE)
    mark_misclassified(ax, X, wrong, label=f"Misclassified by the {name} weights")
    ax.set_title(f"Misclassified points marked for the {name} weights (accuracy {acc:.2%})")
    ax.legend(loc="upper left", framealpha=0.95, fontsize=9)
fig.suptitle("Figure 5 - Final and pocket decision boundaries on the overlapping data", fontsize=14)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIGURES / "fig5_boundaries.png", dpi=150)
plt.close(fig)

epochs = np.arange(0, history.epochs + 1)
current_curve = np.array([initial_accuracy] + history.accuracy) * 100   # epoch 0 = initial weights
best_curve = np.array([initial_accuracy] + history.best_accuracy) * 100

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
ax.plot(epochs, current_curve, color="#d62728", linewidth=1.3, marker="o", markersize=2.5,
        label="Current weights (end of each epoch)")
ax.plot(epochs, best_curve, color="#2ca02c", linewidth=2.2, drawstyle="steps-post",
        label="Best so far (pocket)")
ax.axhline(bayes_accuracy * 100, color="black", linestyle=":", linewidth=1.2,
           label=f"Reference: Bayes line $x_1 + x_2 = 7$ ({bayes_accuracy:.2%})")
ax.axhline(50, color="grey", linestyle="--", linewidth=1, label="Chance level (50%)")
ax.set_xlabel("Epoch")
ax.set_ylabel("Accuracy on the full dataset (%)")
ax.set_title(f"Figure 6 - Accuracy $\\times$ epoch on the overlapping data ($\\eta = {ETA}$)")
ax.set_ylim(40, 80)
ax.grid(alpha=0.25, linestyle=":")
ax.legend(loc="lower right", framealpha=0.95)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIGURES / "fig6_accuracy.png", dpi=150)
plt.close(fig)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# D - Analysis: where the final boundary sits, and why the loop leaves it there
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
norms = np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1)
centre = X.mean(axis=0)
updates = np.array(history.updates)                        # (epochs, 2): class 0, class 1
w_norms = np.linalg.norm(np.array(history.w), axis=1)

# Every update moves b by exactly +eta or -eta, so b_final = b0 + eta * (class-1 - class-0 updates).
b_walk = ETA * (updates[:, 1].sum() - updates[:, 0].sum())

# One mistake on x shifts the score w.x' + b of EVERY point x' by eta * e * (x . x' + 1).
# Compare the size of that shift with how spread out the scores of the data are.
score_jump = ETA * float(np.mean(X @ centre + 1))           # shift of a typical point, for a typical x
final_scores = X @ final_w + final_b

# Inside each epoch: the state right after the class-0 block against the state at its end.
replayed = replay_training(w0, 0.0, ETA, X, y, history)
mid_pred1 = np.array([np.mean(step(X @ w + b)) for _, (w, b), _ in replayed])
end_pred1 = np.array([np.mean(step(X @ w + b)) for _, _, (w, b) in replayed])
mid_acc = np.array([np.mean(step(X @ w + b) == y) for _, (w, b), _ in replayed])
mistake_positions = [i for mistakes, _, _ in replayed for i in mistakes]
n_on_block_start = sum(i in (0, N_PER_CLASS) for i in mistake_positions)


def run(eta, max_epochs, X_run=X, y_run=y):
    """Train a fresh copy of the same perceptron from the same w0; used by the checks below."""
    m = Perceptron(w0, 0.0, eta)
    h = m.fit(X_run, y_run, max_epochs=max_epochs)
    return m, h


# More epochs? A smaller eta? Both, from the same w0 and the same data.
checks = [(ETA, MAX_EPOCHS, model, history)]
for eta, max_epochs in ((ETA, 1000), (0.001, MAX_EPOCHS), (0.001, 1000)):
    checks.append((eta, max_epochs, *run(eta, max_epochs)))

# Is the ~50% an artefact of presenting the classes in two blocks? Shuffle and look again.
# (Drawn from the same rng AFTER everything above, so none of the reported numbers move.)
perm = rng.permutation(len(X))
shuffled_once, history_shuffled_once = run(ETA, MAX_EPOCHS, X[perm], y[perm])

reshuffled = Perceptron(w0, 0.0, ETA)            # a fresh permutation every epoch
reshuffled_best, reshuffled_stopped = -np.inf, False
for _ in range(MAX_EPOCHS):
    p = rng.permutation(len(X))
    h = reshuffled.fit(X[p], y[p], max_epochs=1)      # one epoch in the new order
    reshuffled_best = max(reshuffled_best, reshuffled.pocket_accuracy)
    if h.converged:
        reshuffled_stopped = True
        break

# Figure 6b: what the flat red curve of Figure 6 hides - the predictions flip every half epoch
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
ax.plot(epochs[1:], end_pred1 * 100, color="#ff7f0e", marker="o", markersize=2.5, linewidth=1.3,
        label="At the end of the epoch (after the class-1 block)")
ax.plot(epochs[1:], mid_pred1 * 100, color="#1f77b4", marker="o", markersize=2.5, linewidth=1.3,
        label="Halfway through the epoch (after the class-0 block)")
ax.set_xlabel("Epoch")
ax.set_ylabel("Points predicted as class 1 (%)")
ax.set_ylim(-5, 105)
ax.set_title("Figure 6b - Share of the 2000 points predicted as class 1, inside each epoch")
ax.grid(alpha=0.25, linestyle=":")
ax.legend(loc="center right", framealpha=0.95)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIGURES / "fig6b_flip.png", dpi=150)
plt.close(fig)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reported numbers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    np.set_printoptions(precision=4, suppress=True)

    print("=" * 78)
    print("EXERCISE 2 - OVERLAPPING DATA")
    print(f"seed = {SEED} | 2 classes x {N_PER_CLASS} samples | order: all class 0, then all class 1")
    print("=" * 78)

    print("\n[A] generating parameters and sample statistics")
    for k, mean in enumerate((MEAN_0, MEAN_1)):
        cloud = X[y == k]
        print(f"  class {k}: mean={mean} cov={COV} | sample mean={cloud.mean(axis=0)}"
              f" sample std={cloud.std(axis=0)}")
    print(f"  ||x|| over the dataset: mean {norms.mean():.4f}, min {norms.min():.4f}, max {norms.max():.4f}")

    print("\n[B] training with the pocket")
    print(f"  w0 = {w0}, b0 = 0.0, accuracy of the initial weights = {initial_accuracy:.4f}")
    print(f"  epochs run = {history.epochs} (converged = {history.converged}); "
          f"updates in the last epoch = {sum(history.updates[-1])}, "
          f"fewest updates in any epoch = {int(updates.sum(axis=1).min())}")
    print(f"  FINAL  w = {final_w}, b = {final_b:.4f}, accuracy = {final_accuracy:.4f}"
          f" ({int(wrong_final.sum())} misclassified)")
    print(f"  POCKET w = {pocket_w}, b = {pocket_b:.4f}, accuracy = {pocket_accuracy:.4f}"
          f" ({int(wrong_pocket.sum())} misclassified), found in epoch {model.pocket_epoch}")
    print(f"  reference: Bayes line x1 + x2 = 7 -> accuracy {bayes_accuracy:.4f} on this sample, "
          f"{bayes_expected:.4f} expected")

    print("\n[C] accuracy per epoch")
    print(f"  current: min {min(history.accuracy):.4f}, max {max(history.accuracy):.4f}, "
          f"mean {np.mean(history.accuracy):.4f}")
    print(f"  current, first 10 epochs: {np.round(history.accuracy[:10], 4).tolist()}")
    print(f"  current, last 10 epochs:  {np.round(history.accuracy[-10:], 4).tolist()}")
    print(f"  best so far at the end of epochs 1, 10, 50, 100: "
          f"{[round(history.best_accuracy[e - 1], 4) for e in (1, 10, 50, 100)]}")

    print("\n[D] where the boundaries sit (offset = -b/||w||, distance from the origin along w)")
    for name, w, b in (("final ", final_w, final_b), ("pocket", pocket_w, pocket_b), ("bayes ", bayes_w, bayes_b)):
        print(f"  {name}: angle of w = {angle_deg(w):7.3f} deg, ||w|| = {np.linalg.norm(w):.4f}, "
              f"offset = {boundary_offset(w, b):.4f}, data centre along w = "
              f"{float(centre @ w / np.linalg.norm(w)):.4f}, predicted class 1 = {np.mean(step(X @ w + b)):.4f}")

    print("\n[D] how far one mistake moves b against w")
    print(f"  |delta b| = eta = {ETA};  ||delta w|| = eta * ||x|| = {ETA * norms.mean():.4f} on average "
          f"(ratio {norms.mean():.2f})")
    print(f"  bias walk: eta * (class-1 updates {int(updates[:, 1].sum())} - class-0 updates "
          f"{int(updates[:, 0].sum())}) = {b_walk:.4f} = final b ({final_b:.4f})")
    print(f"  ||w|| at the end of the epochs: min {w_norms.min():.4f}, max {w_norms.max():.4f} "
          f"(started at {np.linalg.norm(w0):.4f})")
    print(f"  bias needed to put a line with the final w through the data centre: "
          f"{-float(centre @ final_w):.4f} (actual b = {final_b:.4f})")
    print(f"  score shift of a typical point after ONE mistake: eta*(x.x'+1) = {score_jump:.4f}; "
          f"spread (std) of the final scores over the data = {final_scores.std():.4f}")

    print("\n[D] inside the epochs (replayed from the states recorded by fit)")
    print(f"  total updates = {len(mistake_positions)} in {history.epochs} epochs; "
          f"{n_on_block_start} of them on the FIRST sample of a class block (index 0 or {N_PER_CLASS})")
    print(f"  updates per epoch: min {int(updates.sum(axis=1).min())}, max {int(updates.sum(axis=1).max())}, "
          f"mean {updates.sum(axis=1).mean():.2f}")
    print(f"  right after the class-0 block: predicted class 1 = {mid_pred1.mean():.4f} on average "
          f"(max {mid_pred1.max():.4f}), accuracy {mid_acc.mean():.4f} on average")
    print(f"  at the end of the epoch:       predicted class 1 = {end_pred1.mean():.4f} on average "
          f"(min {end_pred1.min():.4f}), accuracy {np.mean(history.accuracy):.4f} on average")
    last_mistakes, (w_mid, b_mid), _ = replayed[-1]
    print(f"  last epoch: updates at samples {last_mistakes}; after the class-0 block w = {w_mid}, "
          f"b = {b_mid:.4f}, offset = {boundary_offset(w_mid, b_mid):.4f}, "
          f"predicted class 1 = {np.mean(step(X @ w_mid + b_mid)):.4f}")

    print("\n[D] more epochs / smaller eta (same data, same w0)")
    print("| eta | epochs | final accuracy | pocket accuracy | updates in the last epoch |")
    print("|---|---|---|---|---|")
    for eta, max_epochs, m, h in checks:
        print(f"| {eta} | {h.epochs} | {m.accuracy(X, y):.4f} | {m.pocket_accuracy:.4f} "
              f"| {sum(h.updates[-1])} |")

    print("\n[D] sample order (same data, same w0, eta = 0.01, 100 epochs)")
    print(f"  shuffled once:        final {shuffled_once.accuracy(X, y):.4f}, pocket "
          f"{shuffled_once.pocket_accuracy:.4f}, converged = {history_shuffled_once.converged}, "
          f"current accuracy min/max over epochs {min(history_shuffled_once.accuracy):.4f}/"
          f"{max(history_shuffled_once.accuracy):.4f}")
    print(f"  reshuffled per epoch: final {reshuffled.accuracy(X, y):.4f}, best seen "
          f"{reshuffled_best:.4f}, converged = {reshuffled_stopped}")

    print("\n[figures]")
    for name in ("fig4_data.png", "fig5_boundaries.png", "fig6_accuracy.png", "fig6b_flip.png"):
        print(f"  saved {FIGURES / name}")

docs.title: EDA — Stroke Prediction
docs.text:
Luca Santana Feltrin · Eduardo Takei Yaginuma · Gabriel Fernando Missaka Mendes

Insper · Artificial Neural Networks and Deep Learning · 2026.2

This report asks which demographic and recorded health features are associated with the observed stroke label and how to prepare them for a future neural network classification project. It does not train a predictive model. All exploratory analyses after the split use training rows only; test rows are used for split accounting and the required transformation checks.

docs.title: 0. Proposal
docs.text:
The team selected classification with the public, tabular Stroke Prediction Dataset, published by fedesoriano. The team confirms instructor approval of this dataset. The team repository is LucaFeltrin14/ann-dl.

The CSV contains 5,110 rows × 12 columns: an identifier, the target, and 10 predictors (3 numerical and 7 categorical). It meets the minimum of 1,000 instances and five mixed-type features. The same dataset will be retained for the classification deliverable.

Motivation: Mixed demographic and health measurements provide a useful test of neural network preparation: categorical encodings, different numerical scales, missing measurements and a rare positive class coexist in a compact dataset. Studying these properties first allows the later modeling choices to be grounded in evidence.

First risk: Only 249/5,110 = 4.87% of rows have stroke=1; accuracy alone could conceal failure to detect positives. The original sampling frame, measurement timing and collection protocol are not established by the public description, so clinical generalization and prospective prediction cannot be claimed from this file.

docs.title: A. Data dictionary
docs.text:
Source and unit of observation: Each row is a patient record in the published CSV, with a unique id. The public description does not establish the hospital, country, collection date, representative sampling or whether measurements precede the stroke label. This is an analysis of the recorded label, not evidence of future incident stroke prediction.

Table 1. Complete data dictionary. Semantic type takes precedence over storage dtype.

Column Meaning Semantic type / role Unit or values id Record identifier Identifier; excluded Arbitrary integer; no measurement unit gender Recorded gender category Nominal categorical Female, Male, Other age Recorded age Continuous numerical Years; fractional ages retained hypertension Recorded hypertension flag Binary categorical 0=no, 1=yes heart_disease Recorded heart disease flag Binary categorical 0=no, 1=yes ever_married Whether ever married Binary categorical No, Yes work_type Recorded employment category Nominal categorical Private, Self-employed, Govt_job, children, Never_worked Residence_type Recorded residence category Binary categorical Rural, Urban avg_glucose_level Recorded average glucose measurement Continuous numerical Public description does not specify the unit; no conversion assumed bmi Body mass index Continuous numerical kg/m²; N/A parsed as missing smoking_status Recorded smoking category Nominal categorical formerly smoked, never smoked, smokes, Unknown stroke Recorded stroke occurrence Binary categorical target 0=no, 1=yes

The name gender is retained from the source; the single Other record is not treated as an error. The source states that Unknown in smoking status means the information was unavailable: it is a recorded missing-information category, distinct from a literal empty cell. No unsupported unit or medical plausibility cutoff is inferred for glucose.

docs.title: B. Quality
docs.text:
Table 2. Full-file missingness and training missingness by column.

column missing_count missing_pct train_missing_count train_missing_pct unique_nonmissing id 0 0.000 0 0.000 5110 gender 0 0.000 0 0.000 3 age 0 0.000 0 0.000 104 hypertension 0 0.000 0 0.000 2 heart_disease 0 0.000 0 0.000 2 ever_married 0 0.000 0 0.000 2 work_type 0 0.000 0 0.000 5 Residence_type 0 0.000 0 0.000 2 avg_glucose_level 0 0.000 0 0.000 3979 bmi 201 3.933 170 4.159 418 smoking_status 0 0.000 0 0.000 4 stroke 0 0.000 0 0.000 2

The largest missingness is bmi: 201/5,110 = 3.93% in the full file; training has 170/4,088 = 4.16%. Every other column has 0 empty values. In the training data, smoking_status=Unknown is retained and counted in Table 5.

The full-file audit found 0 identical rows, 0 duplicates after removing id, 0 repeated IDs, and **0 constant predictors. Explicit domain checks found 0 ages outside [0,120], 0 nonpositive glucose values, 0 nonpositive observed BMI values, 0 invalid binary flags, and 0 categorical values outside the documented vocabularies. Contextual checks found 0 children records aged ≥18, 0 ever-married records under 18, and **9 current-smoker records under 18. These contextual flags warrant source clarification, not automatic deletion.

Leakage audit and dropped columns: id is dropped because its arbitrary value is not a usable patient measurement; stroke is separated as the target and never enters preprocessing or the projections. No other predictor directly contains the target, and no numerical predictor pair has an absolute correlation ≥0.90 (Table 6). Correlation alone cannot rule out temporal leakage: measurement timing is unknown for every health feature. There is no timestamp for a temporal split; unique IDs support a record split, but cannot prove that undisclosed repeated patients or related records do not exist. These limitations remain modeling risks.

The full-file quality inventory and target counts are the required stage-1 audit. They do not fit imputers, scalers, projections or encoders. The fixed split precedes all data-dependent preprocessing choices and the training analyses below.

docs.title: A. Strategies
docs.text:
These choices prepare the features for a neural network without consuming the test set.

Missing values: BMI is the only column with empty cells (Table 2). Training BMI missingness is 18.59% for stroke=1 versus 3.42% for stroke=0. Dropping incomplete rows could disproportionately remove positives. Impute each numerical feature with its training median, and retain an explicit 0/1 BMI-missing indicator so the absence is not silently equated to an observed median. This pattern may reflect collection practice, so the indicator is also a leakage/generalization risk to review in future modeling. Categorical empty cells, if encountered, use __MISSING__; the observed Unknown smoking category is retained separately. No missing value is filled using the target.

Outliers: Table 11 applies training-only 1.5×IQR fences to observed values. There are 569 distinct flagged training rows (some features can flag the same row). The chosen strategy removes 0 rows and clips 0 values: an IQR flag does not establish an erroneous health measurement, and adult BMI thresholds should not be imposed on a mixed-age sample. Retain the extremes and document their influence; do not delete a minority patient because of an unusual feature. Robust scaling limits the effect of extremes on fitted location and scale, although it does not bound the transformed values or eliminate their effect on PCA.

Table 11. Training outlier fences and counts.

feature lower_fence upper_fence flagged flagged_pct age -26.500 113.500 0 0.000 avg_glucose_level 21.985 169.525 503 12.304 bmi 9.350 47.350 90 2.202

Encoding: The seven nominal predictors (including hypertension and heart disease) have 2–5 categories each (Table 5), making one-hot encoding appropriate without a large vocabulary. Use drop=None: there is no reference-category constraint for a neural network, and observed categories remain explicit. OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") maps an unseen category to an all-zero block and preserves the feature count. This is explicitly checked using a synthetic unseen gender; the real test set need not contain an unseen category to test this contract. Do not target-encode, resample, or balance before the split.

Scaling: The training ranges differ: age 0.08–82.00, glucose 55.12–271.74, and BMI 10.30–97.60 (Table 4), while categorical indicators lie in [0,1]. The observed glucose/BMI right tails and Table 11 motivate RobustScaler, subtracting the training median and dividing by the training IQR after imputation. It helps numerical conditioning without fitting extreme-sensitive mean/variance parameters. One-hot columns and the missingness indicator remain 0/1; scaling every rare binary column to unit variance would amplify rare categories. No additional scaling is fitted on test.

Table 12. Fitted numerical parameters. The scaler IQR uses the imputed training matrix; therefore it can differ from Table 4's observed-value quartiles.

feature imputation_median scaler_center scaler_iqr age 45.000 45.000 35.000 avg_glucose_level 91.945 91.945 36.885 bmi 28.000 28.000 9.000

docs.title: B. Dimensionality reduction
docs.text:
All projections use the same 4,088 training rows and 24 pipeline-output features. Neither stroke nor id enters their fitting; target values are used only for coloring. There is no subsampling for fitting. Euclidean distance is applied to robust-scaled numerical features plus one-hot categories and the BMI-missing indicator. This mixed representation weights continuous and categorical blocks according to this preprocessing choice; its geometry is not a clinical distance. Redundant one-hot blocks can also create zero-variance PCA directions.

PCA: Fit full SVD on the transformed train only. PC1 explains 29.25%, PC2 explains 17.40%, and together they explain 46.65%; 10 components reach 90% cumulative variance. The two displayed components therefore cannot represent all predictive information. PCA centers its input internally; no target enters the decomposition.

Conclusion — Figure 10: The positive records are visually more common toward the higher-glucose arm and the older/higher-BMI portion, but negatives occupy these regions too. PC1 is dominated by glucose (+0.8684); PC2 contrasts BMI (+0.5612) and age (+0.3659) with glucose (-0.4818). The projection preserves only 46.65% of variance and does not demonstrate class separability.

Table 13. Five largest absolute eigenvector coefficients per displayed component. Full coefficients are in results/pca_loadings.csv.

component feature coefficient PC1 num__avg_glucose_level 0.8684 PC1 num__bmi 0.2975 PC1 num__age 0.2572 PC1 cat__ever_married_No -0.1609 PC1 cat__ever_married_Yes 0.1609 PC2 num__bmi 0.5612 PC2 num__avg_glucose_level -0.4818 PC2 num__age 0.3659 PC2 cat__ever_married_No -0.2923 PC2 cat__ever_married_Yes 0.2923

PC1 reading: The largest contributions are num__avg_glucose_level (+0.8684), num__bmi (+0.2975), num__age (+0.2572). Same-sign coefficients move in the same score direction; opposite signs express a contrast. These are eigenvector coefficients, not correlations or feature importance for stroke prediction. Component signs can be reversed without changing the projection's information.

PC2 reading: The largest contributions are num__bmi (+0.5612), num__avg_glucose_level (-0.4818), num__age (+0.3659). Same-sign coefficients move in the same score direction; opposite signs express a contrast. These are eigenvector coefficients, not correlations or feature importance for stroke prediction. Component signs can be reversed without changing the projection's information.

t-SNE: Compare perplexities 30 and 50, with 2 components, Euclidean metric, PCA initialization, learning_rate="auto", 1,000 iterations, and random_state=42. UMAP: Compare n_neighbors 15 and 50, with 2 components, min_dist=0.1, Euclidean metric, spectral initialization, 500 epochs, random_state=42, transform_seed=42 and n_jobs=1. The parameter pairs are sensitivity checks, not an optimization against test labels or target separation.

Conclusion — Figure 11: Both perplexities show many small local groups and a region containing more visible positives, with negative records mixed into it. A clean class boundary is absent at either setting. Trustworthiness is 0.9730 at perplexity 30 and 0.9769 at 50 (Table 14), exceeding PCA's 0.8257 on the same evaluation subset. Island sizes and inter-island distances do not measure original feature-space distances or disease risk.

Conclusion — Figure 12: Both neighborhood sizes show separated local groups and mixed-class regions; their positions and arrangement change markedly between settings. Trustworthiness is 0.9672 at 15 neighbors and 0.9725 at 50 (Table 14). Local organization is better preserved than in 2D PCA, but this metric does not validate the apparent islands or show that stroke is predictable.

Table 14. Projection diagnostics. Trustworthiness (k=10) is evaluated on the same fixed, random 1,000-row subset of training data for all maps; it measures neighborhood preservation within that subset. It is not a classification score. t-SNE KL divergence is an optimization diagnostic; comparing its values across perplexities does not identify a predictive winner.

method parameter trustworthiness kl_divergence pca 2 0.8257 — tsne 30 0.9730 0.8359 tsne 50 0.9769 0.8491 umap 15 0.9672 — umap 50 0.9725 —

Comparison: PCA supplies a global linear view with interpretable variance and coefficients. t-SNE and UMAP reveal fragmented local arrangements that can be compressed or superimposed by the first two principal components. Mixed categorical indicators can contribute to these fragments, but target coloring alone does not identify which variable generates them. Their island layouts depend on neighborhood parameters and on the chosen mixed-feature distance. Inspect the two settings together rather than name a single cluster configuration as ground truth. Figure 10 gives the interpretable variance baseline; Figures 11–12 show the extra local detail, and Table 14 quantifies neighborhood distortion. None of these embeddings is used to claim future classifier performance. The pipeline retains the original transformed features for the later modeling deliverable rather than replacing them with a chosen 2D embedding.

docs.title: C. Pipeline
docs.text:
The importable factory build_preprocessor() in code/preprocessing.py returns an unfitted scikit-learn Pipeline containing a ColumnTransformer with numerical, BMI-missing-indicator and categorical branches. eda.py calls fit_transform(X_train) once, and transform(X_test). The target is separate; id is absent from FEATURES.

The final output is train (4088, 24) and test (1022, 24), with 0 training NaNs, 0 test NaNs and zero infinities. The 24 features are three scaled numerical columns, one missingness indicator and 20 one-hot columns. The exact names are reported below and exported in results/feature_names.csv.

docs.title: Findings and risks for the modeling team
docs.text: Finding and evidence Modeling consequence / handling plan Minority class: 249 cases, 4.87% (Table 3; Figure 1) Use stratified validation within training. Report PR-AUC, recall, precision and confusion counts; choose thresholds using validation. Fit class weights or any resampling inside training folds only. Age structure and unadjusted disease/category associations overlap (Tables 7–10; Figures 6–9) Keep the features, investigate confounding and subgroup behavior during validation; avoid causal or diagnostic claims from EDA. BMI missingness is more frequent among positives (Table 2; section 4A) Keep median imputation and the indicator; compare validation behavior with/without the indicator and investigate recording-time leakage. Glucose and BMI have right tails; 569 rows are flagged by IQR (Tables 4 and 11; Figure 2) Retain the rows, use robust scaling and inspect training-fold sensitivity to extreme values; never select cutoffs from test outcomes. Rare categories and unavailable smoking information (Table 5; Figure 3) Preserve documented categories; handle new categories explicitly and monitor their frequency. One training record cannot support a gender-specific conclusion. Strongest numerical pair is moderate, not redundant (Table 6; Figures 4–5) Keep all three numerical predictors; do not turn an exploratory rank correlation into automatic feature selection. PCA loses information and nonlinear maps vary with settings (Figures 10–12; Tables 13–14) Use projections to inspect geometry, keep the full pipeline features for modeling, and evaluate any later dimension reduction within validation folds. Collection provenance and feature timing are not established (sections 0 and 1) Treat the task as classification of recorded labels. Obtain provenance and longitudinal timing before claiming future risk prediction or clinical validity.

"""Importable, unfitted preprocessing for the Stroke Prediction classification task.

No estimator is fitted during import. Call build_preprocessor(), fit it on X_train,
and only transform X_test. Binary clinical flags are nominal features, not counts.
"""
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.impute import MissingIndicator, SimpleImputer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, RobustScaler

SEED = 42
NUMERIC_FEATURES = ["age", "avg_glucose_level", "bmi"]
CATEGORICAL_FEATURES = [
    "gender", "hypertension", "heart_disease", "ever_married", "work_type",
    "Residence_type", "smoking_status",
]
FEATURES = NUMERIC_FEATURES + CATEGORICAL_FEATURES


def build_preprocessor() -> Pipeline:
    """Return a fresh Pipeline; output is a dense, finite numeric matrix.

    The explicit BMI indicator is never scaled (its values stay 0/1). Missing
    categories use a distinct sentinel; the literal smoking category Unknown
    remains an observed category. Unknown categories at transform time produce
    an all-zero one-hot block and never trigger fitting on the held-out rows.
    """
    columns = ColumnTransformer([
        ("num", Pipeline([
            ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median", keep_empty_features=True)),
            ("scale", RobustScaler(quantile_range=(25, 75))),
        ]), NUMERIC_FEATURES),
        ("bmi_missing", MissingIndicator(features="all", error_on_new=False), ["bmi"]),
        ("cat", Pipeline([
            ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value="__MISSING__")),
            ("encode", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False,
                                     dtype=float, drop=None)),
        ]), CATEGORICAL_FEATURES),
    ], remainder="drop", verbose_feature_names_out=True)
    return Pipeline([("columns", columns)])

    assert_allclose(columns.named_transformers_["num"]["impute"].statistics_,medians)
    imputed = train[NUM].fillna(dict(zip(NUM,medians))).to_numpy()
    center = np.median(imputed,axis=0)
    q1,q3 = np.quantile(imputed,[.25,.75],axis=0)
    assert_allclose(Xt[:,:3],(imputed-center)/(q3-q1))
    assert_array_equal(Xt[:,3],train.bmi.isna().to_numpy().astype(float))
    fitted_num = csv("fitted_numeric")
    assert_allclose(fitted_num.imputation_median,medians)
    assert_allclose(fitted_num.scaler_center,center)
    assert_allclose(fitted_num.scaler_iqr,q3-q1)
    encoder = columns.named_transformers_["cat"]["encode"]
    assert sum(map(len,encoder.categories_)) == 20
    for c,categories_ in zip(CAT,encoder.categories_):
        assert set(categories_) == set(train[c].unique())
    # Deliberately shift only held-out inputs; training state and output must stay fixed.
    changed = Xtest.copy()
    changed[NUM] = changed[NUM].fillna(0)+10000
    changed["gender"] = "UNSEEN_GENDER"
    transformed = pipeline.transform(changed)
    assert np.isfinite(transformed).all()
    assert state == pickle.dumps(pipeline)
    assert_allclose(pipeline.transform(Xtrain),Xt)
    gender_indices = [i for i,n in enumerate(pipeline.get_feature_names_out()) if n.startswith("cat__gender_")]
    assert_allclose(transformed[:,gender_indices],0)
    probe = Xtest.iloc[:4].copy()
    probe[NUM] = np.nan
    probe["smoking_status"] = np.nan
    probe["gender"] = "UNSEEN_GENDER"
    out = pipeline.transform(probe)
    assert out.shape == (4,24) and np.isfinite(out).all()
    assert_allclose(out[:,gender_indices],0)
    assert_array_equal(out[:,3],np.ones(4))
    assert state == pickle.dumps(pipeline)

    # Independent NumPy SVD verifies PCA explained variance and coefficients.
    _, singular, right = np.linalg.svd(Xt-Xt.mean(axis=0),full_matrices=False)
    variance_ratio = singular**2 / np.sum(singular**2)
    pca = csv("pca_variance")
    assert_allclose(pca.explained_ratio,variance_ratio,atol=1e-9,rtol=1e-8)
    assert_allclose(pca.cumulative_ratio,np.cumsum(variance_ratio),atol=1e-9)
    assert_allclose(m["pca_pc1_pc2"],variance_ratio[:2].sum())
    assert m["pca_components_90"] == np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(variance_ratio),.9)+1
    loads = csv("pca_loadings")
    for i,pc in enumerate(["PC1","PC2"]):
        assert_allclose(np.abs(loads[pc]),np.abs(right[i]),atol=1e-8)
    diagnostics = csv("projection_diagnostics")
    eval_idx = np.sort(np.random.default_rng(42).choice(len(Xt),size=1000,replace=False))
    for method in ["pca","tsne_30","tsne_50","umap_15","umap_50"]:
        embedding = csv(f"embedding_{method}")
        assert_array_equal(embedding.id,train.id)
        assert_array_equal(embedding.stroke,train.stroke)
        assert embedding.shape == (4088,4)
        assert np.isfinite(embedding[["dimension1","dimension2"]]).all().all()
        xy = embedding[["dimension1","dimension2"]].to_numpy()
        method_name,parameter = ("pca",2) if method=="pca" else (method.split("_")[0],int(method.split("_")[1]))
        diagnostic = diagnostics[(diagnostics.method==method_name)&(diagnostics.parameter==parameter)].iloc[0]
        score = trustworthiness(Xt[eval_idx],xy[eval_idx],n_neighbors=10)
        assert_allclose(diagnostic.trustworthiness,score,atol=1e-6)
        if method=="pca":
            assert_allclose(xy,(Xt-Xt.mean(axis=0)) @ loads[["PC1","PC2"]].to_numpy(),atol=1e-8,rtol=1e-8)
    assert len(csv("projection_diagnostics")) == 5
    assert csv("projection_diagnostics").trustworthiness.between(0,1).all()

    report = (BASE / "index.md").read_text()
    for key in ["project: eda","task: classification","ai_use:","Luca Santana Feltrin",
                "Eduardo Takei Yaginuma","Gabriel Fernando Missaka Mendes"]:
        assert key in report
    assert [int(x) for x in re.findall(r"^## ([0-5])\.",report,re.M)] == list(range(6))
    sections = re.split(r"^## ",report,flags=re.M)
    for number in [2,3]:
        section = next(s for s in sections if s.startswith(f"{number}."))
        for item in re.split(r"^### ",section,flags=re.M)[1:]:
            assert len(re.findall(r"!\[Figure",item)) <= 3
    figures = re.findall(r"!\[Figure (\d+)\.[^\]]*\]\((figures/[^)]+)\)",report)
    assert [int(n) for n,_ in figures] == list(range(1,13))
    for number,path in figures:
        assert (BASE / path).is_file()
        assert f"Conclusion — Figure {number}:" in report
    summary = report.split("### Results summary\n",1)[1]
    rows = re.findall(r"^\| (\d+) \|",summary,re.M)
    assert list(map(int,rows)) == list(range(1,11))
    assert summary.strip().endswith("|")
    assert f"{m['pca_pc1_pc2']*100:.2f}%" in summary
    assert f"ρ={m['strongest_pair']['spearman']:.4f}" in summary
    for name in pipeline.get_feature_names_out():
        assert name in report
    print("PASS: source/checksum; all split, quality, target, numerical, category, correlation,")
    print("outlier and grouped statistics; train-only fitted parameters; held-out perturbation;")
    print("missing/unseen-category contract; independent PCA SVD; embedding IDs; report structure,")
    print("all 12 figures and conclusions; feature names; all 10 results-summary rows.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
